#### Observation 6203: stage verse-reading, tag answered-no-flag, status withdrawn, deleted 1

- strong: G2212; window: meaning; created_at: 2026-09-18T12:11:08Z; updated_at: 2026-09-23T08:55:03Z
- **obs_text:** The full vocabulary arc of zeteo spans from concrete physical searching (hunting, looking for a lost object), through judicial/philosophical inquiry and questioning, to volitional striving/desiring, to the idiomatic 'seek the life of' meaning to hunt down and kill. Across this batch it is used for hostile pursuit-to-kill (John 7:1,19,25,30; 8:40; 10:39; Acts 21:31), for self-interested pursuit of glory (John 7:18), for existential/futile seeking (John 7:34), for religious groping toward God (Acts 17:27), and for self-preservation (Acts 27:30, sailors seeking to escape). The range is thus morally and relationally neutral in itself -- its valence is set entirely by its object and agent.

#### Observation 7056: stage char-reading, tag tightly-related, status draft, deleted 0

- strong: G1567; window: Subgroup; created_at: 2026-09-18T12:36:38Z
- **obs_text:** G1567 (ekzeteo) and G1934 (epizeteo) both intensify the base zeteo root via a directional prefix (ek- 'out/thoroughly' vs epi- 'upon/toward'), and both share the same semantic split visible cross-strong: a devotional/diligent-seeking sense (ekzeteo: Acts.15.17, Heb.11.6, Rom.3.11, 1Pet.1.10; epizeteo: Heb.11.14, Heb.13.14, Acts.13.7) alongside a demanding/legal-exaction sense (ekzeteo: Luke.11.50-51, blood 'required'; epizeteo: Matt.12.39, Matt.16.4, Mark.8.12, Luke.11.29, demanding a sign; Acts.19.39, formal legal matter). Both Greek terms thus independently develop the same two-pole range (earnest seeking <-> exacting demand) from the same simple root, making them the closest pair in this subgroup.

- **obs_text:** G1934 (epizeteo) shares with G1567 (ekzeteo) the same two-pole range: devotional/aspirational seeking (Heb.11.14 homeland, Heb.13.14 city to come, Rom.11.7 status Israel failed to obtain) versus demanding/exacting (Matt.12.39, Matt.16.4, Mark.8.12, Luke.11.29 demanding a sign; Acts.19.39 legal matter to be settled). #### Observation 7172: stage char-answers, tag answered-no-flag, status draft, deleted 0

- window: origin; created_at: 2026-09-18T12:51:48Z
- **obs_text:** The evidence points to both created design and fallen distortion. The created-design pole appears where seeking God is the proper human posture (Heb.11.6, Ps.63.1, Prov.8.17, Acts.15.17) -- an intended capacity oriented toward God as its fulfillment. The fallen-condition pole appears where seeking is either absent altogether (Rom.3.11, 'no one seeks for God') or twisted into hostile demand (Matt.16.4, testing sign-seeking) or exacted judicially against guilt (Luke.11.50-51). The same capacity for intensive seeking is thus shown as originally God-directed but corruptible into either default neglect or adversarial demand.

- window: meaning; created_at: 2026-09-18T12:51:48Z
- **obs_text:** The characteristic is compound in structure: each member combines a base 'seek' root with an intensifying element -- ekzeteo (ek- 'out/thoroughly' + zeteo), epizeteo (epi- 'upon/toward' + zeteo), and shachar (an inherently intensive root tied etymologically to 'dawn/early,' functioning as a built-in intensifier rather than a compounded prefix). The constituent elements are: (1) the base act of seeking, and (2) an added element of thoroughness, direction, or urgency.

#### Observation 14199: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_132448_748-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T13:29:00Z
- **obs_text:** What it does to those beneath it: Pleading against it before it rises:; Judah: "let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself" (Gen 44:18). The plea is a long retelling of the father's love (44:19–21 onward); Rachel: "Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me" (Gen 31:35). The plea for no anger covers a concealment: she is sitting on the stolen gods (31:34); Reading it as a sign: "If he says, 'Good!' it will be well with your servant, but if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him" (1Sa 20:7). Saul's anger is to be read as the evidence of Saul's intent. Jonathan's knowledge follows the same path: after the spear, "Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death" (20:33); Anticipating it and scripting a reply: Joab to the messenger: "if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city?' … then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also'" (2Sa 11:20–21). The anger is foreseen, and so is the one sentence that will turn it. That sentence works because the king had wanted Uriah dead. The line manages the king's anger by exposing the king's own secret; Plotting against it from below: "Bigthan and Teresh … became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus" (Est 2:21). This is anger rising from the servants, discovered through Mordecai (2:22); Anger acting covertly: Zebul, "when [he] heard the words of Gaal … his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly" (Judg 9:30–31). Anger turned into an ambush plan, "set an ambush in the field" (9:32); A group overrules its king: "the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him … 'Send the man back … how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord?'" (1Sa 29:4). The king Achish yields: "Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you" (29:6). The anger comes from suspicion: they fear a loyalty they cannot see.

#### Observation 14224: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_132448_748-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T13:29:00Z
- **obs_text:** Part 2 verses: what they add. Three new strands: (a) The eye wasting, as in Job 17:7; "My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes" (Psa 6:7), after "every night I flood my bed with tears" (6:6); "My eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also. For my life is spent with sorrow" (Psa 31:9–10); The eye is where ka'as shows in the body, in all three texts (Job 17:7; Psa 6:7; 31:9); What turns Psa 6 round is being heard: "the Lord has heard the sound of my weeping. The Lord has heard my plea" (6:8–9). In Psa 10:14, "you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself". The vexation is seen by God, and the helpless hands it over; (b) Provocation from those closest; "A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him" (Pro 17:25); The reverse direction: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger" (Eph 6:4), and "do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Col 3:21); Vexation passes both ways between parent and child. Col 3:21 names its outcome as losing heart. Hannah's rival (1Sa 1:6) was a co-wife. These are the family members; (c) Qoheleth's vexation: the vexation of the thinker and the worker; Knowing brings it: "in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow" (Ecc 1:18). This comes after "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (1:17); Work brings it, and it keeps the heart awake: "his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest" (2:23); "all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger" (5:17); Its answer is enjoyment received as God's gift: "There is nothing better … than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God" (2:24), and "this is the gift of God" (5:19); It is to be removed: "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body" (11:10), after "Rejoice, O young man … let your heart cheer you" (11:9); It is sometimes better than laughter: "Sorrow [ka'as] is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (7:3). The one place where ka'as is valued. The face is sad and the heart made good. Face and heart go in opposite directions.

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_132448_748-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T13:29:00Z
- **obs_text:** Part 2 verses: what they add (both were B8: human vexation induced by God): Paul reads Deu 32:21 as a statement about understanding: "But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, 'I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry'" (Rom 10:19). Then "I have been found by those who did not seek me" (10:20), and "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people" (10:21); The induced anger is set inside God's outstretched hands. It is a provocation meant to bring them back, not only a punishment; Compare Deu 32:29, "If they were wise, they would understand this"; God troubles the nations' hearts at another's fall: "I will trouble [ka'as] the hearts of many peoples, when I bring your destruction among the nations" (Eze 32:9), and "They shall tremble every moment, every one for his own life" (32:10). The vexation God induces comes from seeing a great power fall. It is a trouble of the onlooker, and it turns to fear for one's own life.

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_132928_870-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T13:35:48Z
- **obs_text:** Seat: In the verse: 2Ch 32:25 "his heart was proud" and 32:26 "the pride of his heart". Hezekiah's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.2; D v2 §9.1, §10.1, §11; pilot §2; Outside (all genuine, the bearer's own):; 1Ki 8:47–48 / 2Ch 6:37–38 "turn their heart … with all their heart and with all their soul"; 2Ki 22:19 / 2Ch 34:27 "your heart was penitent / tender"; 2Ch 12:14 "did not set his heart to seek the Lord"; Nothing new in any single seat. What part A adds is a third kind of seat for pilot §2. The pilot has the heart that provokes (the cause) and the spirit that receives (the effect). Part A adds the heart that turns, and so turns the anger away. In these verses, and in §22, it is the human seat most often named in the context of God's anger. For the researcher: whether pilot §2 takes this as a third row.

For if you return … your brothers and your children will find compassion" (2Ch 30:8–9); Separation: "Let our officials stand for the whole assembly … until the fierce wrath of our God over this matter is turned away from us" (Ezr 10:14); Sabbath restored: "Now you are bringing more wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath" (Neh 13:18), then the gates are shut (13:19); Captives released:; Oded: "you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven … Have you not sins of your own against the Lord your God? … send back the captives … for the fierce wrath of the Lord is upon you" (2Ch 28:9–11); The chiefs: "you propose to bring upon us guilt against the Lord in addition to our present sins … there is fierce wrath against Israel" (28:13); Then: "with the spoil they clothed all who were naked among them … provided them with food and drink, and anointed them, and carrying all the feeble among them on donkeys, they brought them to their kinsfolk" (28:15). Fear of adding to the wrath turns into care for enemies who are also kin; Rebuke acted on: "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you … Nevertheless, some good is found in you … you … have set your heart to seek God" (2Ch 19:2–3). Jehoshaphat "went out again among the people … and brought them back to the Lord" (19:4).

Job asks for a hiding place from God's anger in God's own keeping, and expects God to long for him afterwards.

#### Observation 15087: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: read; run_id: RUN-20261026_140621_020-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T14:06:46Z
- **obs_text:** These verses join pride to the turning away from God: Pride is a witness against its owner. "The pride of Israel testifies to his face; yet they do not return to the Lord their God, nor seek him, for all this" (Hos 7:10; also Hos 5:5); It goes with not knowing. The verse before says "Strangers devour his strength, and he knows it not; gray hairs are sprinkled upon him, and he knows it not" (Hos 7:9). In Hos 5:4–5, "they know not the Lord" stands next to "The pride of Israel testifies to his face"; Pride does not listen; "Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the Lord has spoken" (Jer 13:15). The opposite of pride here is hearing; Then: "if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride" (13:17); The pride God will "spoil" belongs to a people "who refuse to hear my words, who stubbornly follow their own heart" (13:9–10); Pride leaves a cry unanswered; "There they cry out, but he does not answer, because of the pride of evil men" (Job 35:12); The cry has no turning to God in it: "none says, 'Where is God my Maker'" (35:10); I read: this cry is a cry of pain that does not seek God; God works to keep pride from a man. He speaks "in a dream ... that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man; he keeps back his soul from the pit" (Job 33:15–18). God's warning is aimed at pride before it ripens; The wicked does not see. "If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness ... and does not see the majesty of the Lord" (Isa 26:10). Not seeing God's majesty sits in the same verse as not learning from his favour.

#### Observation 15195: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_140736_363-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T14:07:58Z
- **obs_text:** The boast is not removed. It is moved: The command. "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31; 2Co 10:17). This follows Christ "who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1:30). It is joined to "it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends" (2Co 10:18); What to boast in; "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24); The boast is in knowing God, and what is known is his character; The soul's boast. "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psa 34:2, carried); Not in my bow. "For not in my bow do I trust ... In God we have boasted continually" (Psa 44:6–8). The psalm then turns: "But you have rejected us" (44:9). The boast in God is kept in the psalm even while the defeat is brought before him; His name. "Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice!" (Psa 105:3; 1Ch 16:10); The worm. "Fear not, you worm Jacob ... you shall rejoice in the Lord; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory" (Isa 41:14–16). The one called a worm is the one who glories; Justified and glorying. "Only in the Lord, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength ... In the Lord all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory" (Isa 45:24–25); The nations. If Israel returns and swears in truth, "nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory" (Jer 4:2); Exulting; "all who swear by him shall exult" (Psa 63:11); "Let the righteous one rejoice in the Lord and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!" (Psa 64:10); "that I may glory with your inheritance" (Psa 106:5); The cross. "far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world" (Gal 6:14); Christ, not the flesh. "glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh — though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also" (Php 3:3–4). Paul has standing in the flesh, "I have more", and sets it aside; Hope, sufferings, God. ESV renders kauchaomai "rejoice" here:; "we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings" (Rom 5:2–3); "we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation" (5:11); The same word that elsewhere is a proud boast is here joy in hope, in suffering, and in God; Held fast. "if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope" (Heb 3:6); The conscience. "our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God" (2Co 1:12). The boast is a clear conscience, and its ground is named as grace.

#### Observation 15205: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: read; run_id: RUN-20261026_140758_537-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T14:08:28Z
- **obs_text:** Proverbs paints the scoffer by what he will not receive: Rebuke; "A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke" (Pro 13:1); "A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12). The verse before is "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the Lord; how much more the hearts of the children of man!" (15:11); Hatred of correction. "Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse ... Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you" (Pro 9:7–8). The same rebuke brings out hate in one and love in the other; Wisdom in vain. "A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding" (Pro 14:6). He seeks, and does not find; Learning by his fall; "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence" (19:25); "When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise" (21:11); The scoffer is not the one who learns. Others learn from what happens to him; Strife. "Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease" (Pro 22:10). "the scoffer is an abomination to mankind" (24:9); Justice and the guilt offering; "A worthless witness mocks at justice" (19:28). "Condemnation is ready for scoffers" (19:29); "Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance" (14:9). They mock the very means of putting guilt right; Delight, and the offer. "How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing ... If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you" (Pro 1:22–23). Scoffing is a delight held on to, and the offer still stands to the one who turns; Alone. "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it" (Pro 9:12); The seat. "Blessed is the man who ... nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord" (Psa 1:1–2). The scoffer's seat is set against delight in the law; The warning; "do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong", then "Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23). Again the opposite of scoffing is hearing; "the scoffer cease ... who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate" (Isa 29:20–21). The scoffer works against the one who reproves. In the same passage "The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord" (29:19); Wine and company; "Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise" (Pro 20:1); "the princes became sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers", and "none of them calls upon me" (Hos 7:5, 7); In Job's debates; Zophar: "when you mock, shall no one shame you?" (Job 11:3); Job: "after I have spoken, mock on" (21:3); Elihu: "Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing" (36:18); I read: the charge of scoffing is thrown between the speakers. As with Eliab in batch 2, the verses do not settle that it is true of Job; "Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor" (Pro 3:34, carried). This is the source of Jam 4:6 and 1Pe 5:5.

- basis: read; run_id: RUN-20261026_142827_567-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T14:29:00Z
- **obs_text:** The humble seek: "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:3). Those already called humble are told to seek humility. I read: in this verse humility is not a thing held once and for all. The humble keep seeking it, under the threat of the day of anger (2:2); "I will leave in your midst a people humble and lowly. They shall seek refuge in the name of the Lord" (Zep 3:12). They are left after God removes "your proudly exultant ones" (3:11). They are described by what they do and do not do: "they shall do no injustice and speak no lies" (3:13); "The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the Lord" (Psa 22:26) and "you who seek God, let your hearts revive" (Psa 69:32). In both, the humble or afflicted stand beside "those who seek". (Psa 22:26 is the afflicted sense, group VI.).

#### Observation 16085: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: read; run_id: RUN-20261026_152029_065-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T15:22:23Z
- **obs_text:** What the sequences show [Claude reading]: The oath marks adherence at a cost.; Elisha's triple oath is the price of the double spirit.; The Shunammite uses Elisha's own oath against him. Her bitterness of soul becomes a hold on the prophet that he cannot refuse.; Uriah's oath by David's soul is kept against David's wish. The wine that should have lowered his guard fails (a failed threshold — Batch F §7). He dies for keeping it.; The oath by the soul can guard a life while refusing a life. Zedekiah swears secretly by "who made our souls" to spare Jeremiah's life. He then declines the life offered to him (38:17, 20), from fear (38:19). The oath and the refusal are in one conversation.; 1Sa 17:55 stands on the threshold of 18:1. A formal oath by Saul's soul immediately precedes the knitting of Jonathan's soul to David's.; The oath misused: "As the Lord lives, I will run after him and get something from him" (Gehazi, 2Ki 5:20; §13.2).; Revisit (Batch H): God swears by his own soul: "The Lord God has sworn by himself [*his nephesh*]" (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14; read in Batch D and E). The oath by a *nephesh* is used of God as well as of men.; The oath answers a claim of vengeance. The murderers of Ish-bosheth: "your enemy, who sought your life. The Lord has avenged my lord the king" (2Sa 4:8). David: "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity" → he has them killed (4:9–12). The oath on David's own redeemed soul refuses a vengeance done on his behalf (Batch H §1.4).; Revisit (delta) — the oath with death in view: The oath formula frames the nearness of death. "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1Sa 20:3). The oath by Jonathan's soul carries David's own peril.; A life pledged for a life. Rahab asks: "swear to me by the Lord … deliver our lives from death" (Jos 2:12–13). The spies answer: "Our life for yours even to death!" (2:14). They do not swear by the Lord's life. They pledge their own *nephesh*.; An oath on a life, broken after a spirit comes (context 1Sa 19:4–12): Jonathan: "he took his life in his hand and struck down the Philistine … Why then will you sin against innocent blood?" (5); "Saul listened … Saul swore, 'As the Lord lives, he shall not be put to death'" (6); War again; David's victory (8); "a harmful spirit from the Lord came upon Saul" (9) [O]

#### Observation 16211: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: read; run_id: RUN-20261026_152029_065-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T15:22:23Z
- **obs_text:** 16.10 Life risked "to death" for others — the OT precedent: "Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death" (Judg 5:18). This is in the same song as "March on, my soul, with might!" (5:21; §3.2).; "Our life for yours even to death!" (Jos 2:14; §4 revisit); David "took his life in his hand" against the Philistine (1Sa 19:5); The men to David: "If half of us die, they will not care [*set heart*] about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us" (2Sa 18:3). The enemy's heart is indifferent to many deaths. One life is weighed at ten thousand.; "the men who were seeking your life are dead" (Exo 4:19) → Moses returns (4:20). The death of the hunters frees the hunted life.; "Why then are you laying a trap for my life to bring about my death?" (1Sa 28:9). This is the medium to the disguised Saul.; "we are about to bring great disaster upon ourselves [*our souls*]" (Jer 26:19). To put the prophet to death would harm the souls of those who kill him. It is set against Hezekiah, who "feared the Lord … and the Lord relented".; [Claude reading] Batch F §3.2 read "hating one's life" and "not loving one's life unto death" as NT discipleship. The OT already has the same shape in battle and in covenant pledges: the life risked "to the death" for a people, a household or a king. What the NT adds is the object, "for the name of the Lord Jesus" (Act 21:13), and the example, "poured out his soul to death" (Isa 53:12).

#### Observation 16837: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: read; run_id: RUN-20261026_153356_055-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T15:35:10Z
- **obs_text:** Jeremiah's sequence — context read, Jer 20:7–14: "you have deceived me" (7); "there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones … I cannot [hold it in]" (9); "my close friends, watching for my fall … 'take our revenge on him'" (10); → "let me see your vengeance … to you have I committed my cause" (12); → "Sing to the Lord; praise the Lord! For he has delivered the life of the needy" (13); → "Cursed be the day on which I was born!" (14); Jer 11:18–21 has the same prayer, and names "the men of Anathoth, who seek your life" (21).; [Claude reading]; Vengeance changes value with the heart that holds it. In the Philistines' soul it is malice. In God's heart it stands in one line with redemption (Isa 63:4). To the anxious heart it is rescue (Isa 35:4).; The prophet's heart does not take vengeance; it hands vengeance over. The friends want "our revenge" (20:10). Jeremiah asks to *see* God's (20:12). The handing over ("to you have I committed my cause") is what makes the praise of 20:13 possible. Two verses later the heart falls to cursing its birth (20:14). The inner seat swings from fire, to entrusting, to praise, to despair in five verses (cf. the despairing soul, Batch G §6).; What follows the divine heart's vengeance is complaint (Isa 63:15–17): the people ask where God's compassion has gone and why he makes them wander (§4.2).

#### Observation 16995: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_153849_636-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T15:40:40Z
- **obs_text:** 0. Data notes: Pre-filters from the handoff do not apply here. None of "Holy Spirit" (M61), "declares the Lord" (M42) or "Lord of hosts" (M72) falls in Batch C clusters. Nothing was removed.; "Seek my life" is one idiom, not inner seeking. About 40 of the 96 M83 verses are *biqqēš nephesh* — "seek (someone's) life" (1Sa 20:1; 23:15; 1Ki 19:10, 14; Jer 11:21; 19:7; 21:7; 22:25; 34:20–21; 44:30; 46:26; 49:37; Psa 35:4; 38:12; 40:14; 54:3; 63:9; 70:2; 86:14; Mat 2:20; Rom 11:3; etc.). Here *nephesh* is life as the object of hostile pursuit. It is reported in §7.5 and not mixed with the soul that seeks.; "Lacks sense" is "lacking heart" (H2638 + H3820A, d1): Pro 7:7; 9:4, 16; 10:13, 21; 11:12; 12:11; 15:21; 17:18; 24:30; 6:32; Ecc 10:3. H2638 "lacking" is filed under M18 Desire. It is a lack, not a desire. See §1.5. → Ruling R1.; "Pleasant" (H2896A *ṭôv*) is mostly generic "good / better". It accounts for 59 M18 pairs. The inner-being uses ("glad / merry / good of heart", "good to the soul", "better … in spirit") are kept in §1.6. Generic "better" is noted and not used (Num 11:18; Judg 9:2; Dan 1:15; 2Sa 18:3; Gen 1:21).; "Striving after wind" (H7469 *reʿût rûaḥ* "longing/pursuit" + rûaḥ *wind*, d1) is the Ecclesiastes refrain (Ecc 1:14; 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 6; 6:9). It is correctly a desire + wind pairing. See §1.9.; "Whole heart" is *lēv shālēm* (H8003 "complete", d1). It is filed under M34 Patience. In the verses it means an undivided, integral heart, not endurance. See §5.1. → Ruling R2.; "Contrite" (H1793A) is filed under M11 Turning. The verses are about a crushed spirit and heart (Psa 34:18; Isa 57:15), not about turning. They are kept in §8.4. → Ruling R3.; Misfiled tags, noted and not used: H6569 "refuse" = *dung*, read as "refuse" (M30): the flesh-skin-dung-burned sacrificial verses (Exo 29:14; Lev 4:11; 8:17; 16:27; Num 19:5); also Eze 32:5 "carcass" and Job 41:23 "folds of his flesh".; H0014 "be willing" filed under M30 because it appears as "would not" (1Ch 11:19; 2Sa 23:17 "he would not drink it"). It is kept only where it is the heart's or spirit's refusal (Exo 10:27; Deu 2:30; Eze 3:7).; "As you yourself live, I will not leave you" (2Ki 2:2, 4, 6; 4:30): an oath formula. H5800A "leave" → M30.; Gen 2:24 "leave … one flesh" → M30.

- **obs_text:** 3. (a) Why the verses were not narrated: The reason is the same as for M47. The M25 units read the life and death words. The desire side of each verse was left for this strand. The M25 ledgers often quote the verse in full, but they quote it for its life or death word: Psa 34:12, "desires life", is quoted for "long days" (LD-101).; Joh 4:14, "never be thirsty again", is quoted for "living water" (LD-121).; Ecc 5:18, "find enjoyment", is quoted for "life enjoyed, as given" (LD-115). That ledger line was woven into Ch 2. 10.6 gained Ecc 2:24–26 in the M47 pass, but not the three verses that say the same thing (3:12; 5:18; 8:15).; Three verses (Exo 14:12, Psa 34:12, Pro 8:35–36) also have a Ch 2 side. I first treated Ch 2 as closed to them. That was my over-reading of OT-08, corrected in §6.

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_163112_087-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T16:32:24Z
- **obs_text:** What they add: Lost and perishing are one word. The lost sheep, coin and son of Luk 15 (15:4, 8, 24, 32), "to seek and to save the lost" (Luk 19:10), "should not perish" (Joh 3:16), and the lost sheep of Israel (Psa 119:176; Jer 50:6; Eze 34:4, 16; Mat 10:6; 15:24). In Luk 15:24 the father sets "dead" beside "lost". Woven in *Death spoken of in more than one way*.; Perishing as a present state, set against being saved. 1Co 1:18; 2Co 2:15; 4:3; 2Th 2:10, with its stated cause: "because they refused to love the truth". Set against it is eternal life (Joh 3:16; 10:28). Woven in the same subsection.; Inner things perish. Hope (Job 8:13; Pro 10:28; Lam 3:18; Eze 19:5; 37:11), courage, literally the heart (Jer 4:9), wisdom and counsel (Isa 29:14; Jer 49:7; Eze 7:26), truth (Jer 7:28), and the heart corrupted by a bribe (Ecc 7:7). Woven in *Death in the living*.; One person destroying another. 1Co 8:11; Rom 14:15. Woven in *Death in the living*, with a pointer to 10.10.; Stated causes of perishing. Forgetting God and serving other gods (Deu 8:19–20; 30:18; Jos 23:16); not repenting (Luk 13:3, 5); not believing (Jude 5); desires to be rich (1Ti 6:9); "those who are far from you shall perish" (Psa 73:27); taking the sword (Mat 26:52); false witness (Pro 19:9; 21:28). Luk 13:3 and 2Th 2:10 are woven. The rest are carried by the death-in-the-living causes and stay here as sources for when those strands are read.; Readiness. "if I perish, I perish" (Est 4:16), woven in *Dying to the Lord*. "The righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart" (Isa 57:1), woven in *Those left behind*.; Not woven, for their strands: losing one's life to find it (Mat 10:39; 16:25; Mar 8:35; 17:33), which is Ch 5's; Luk 9:25 is pointed to from *Dying to the Lord*; "Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?" (Mar 4:38; Mat 8:25; Luk 8:24), cited in 10.12; Jon 1:6, 14; 3:9, which are 10.13's and 13.1's

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_164113_300-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T16:41:39Z
- **obs_text:** Hiding from people: Much of the hiding in Scripture is from people who could do harm, and in these verses it is the weaker side that hides. "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). "The poor of the earth all hide themselves" (Job 24:4). When Israel hid in the caves, "all the people followed him trembling" (1 Samuel 13:7).; Often the verse records not the feeling of the one who hides but someone else's counsel to hide.; Jonathan: "Saul my father seeks to kill you … Stay in a secret place and hide yourself" (1 Samuel 19:2).; God to Elijah: "hide yourself by the brook Cherith" (1 Kings 17:3).; Where the feeling is named, it is fear.; Jacob fled from Laban "secretly", and he said why: "Because I was afraid" (Genesis 31:27, 31).; Joseph of Arimathea was "a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews". The same verse ends with him going to Pilate and taking away the body (John 19:38).; Hiding can be good sense: "The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it" (Proverbs 22:3). It ends when the news changes. The men who had hidden in the hills "heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle" (1 Samuel 14:22).; And sometimes hiding is refused, or impossible.; The servant chooses not to hide: "I gave my back to those who strike … I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting" (Isaiah 50:6).; No one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend" (Psalm 55:12–13).

- **obs_text:** (a) The fugitive hunted to death.; Verses: 1Sa 19:2; 20:5, 19, 24; 23:19, 23; 26:1; Psa 54:1 (David); Judg 9:5 (Jotham); 2Sa 17:9 (David, as Hushai pictures him); 1Ki 17:3 (Elijah); Jer 36:19 (Baruch and Jeremiah); Jos 2:16 (the spies); Jos 10:16, 17, 27 (five kings); 2Ch 22:9 (Ahaziah); Joh 8:59; 12:36 (Jesus).; Where it comes from: a stated threat to life. "Saul my father seeks to kill you" (1Sa 19:2); Abimelech "killed his brothers … But Jotham … hid himself" (Judg 9:5); "they picked up stones to throw at him" (Joh 8:59).; The feeling of the one who hides is almost never stated. What is stated is someone else's counsel to hide: Jonathan (1Sa 19:2), Rahab (Jos 2:16), the officials (Jer 36:19), and God (1Ki 17:3). In this strand the inner operation that shows is the counsellor's: foresight and concern for the other.; What it leads to: survival (Jotham; David), or capture and death (Ahaziah, "captured while hiding", 2Ch 22:9; the five kings, Jos 10:17, 27).

#### Observation 19201: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_164719_204-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T16:49:06Z
- **obs_text:** Seat.; In the verse: 2Ch 22:9 "heart". The word has a genuine inner-being sense, but the heart is Jehoshaphat's, the dead grandfather's: "who sought the Lord with all his heart". Ahaziah, the one hiding, has no seat. Spurious for this phenomenon (v1 §0). Batch C v3 §7.1 read it as seeking the Lord with the heart. Batch G v3 §16.11 read it as "a dead man honoured for his grandfather's heart". Both readings stand. Neither concerns hiding.; Whose seat: none of the 40 hiders has one. In strand (a) the inner operation belongs to the counsellor, and it is shown by what the counsellor says, not by a seat word (v2, kept above).; Outside the verse — new in v3. In strand (a), the nearest seat word is *nephesh* in its life sense: the life being hunted. David, in the psalm headed by the Ziphites' report that he is "hiding among us" (Psa 54:1), says "the Lord is the upholder of my life" (54:4). The seat word names what is at stake in the hiding, not where the hider feels it. This fits Batch G v3 §5 ("Life spared, life hunted — the *nephesh* as a prize"), which it does not change.; Strand (f), prudence — new in v3: Pro 22:3 ("The prudent sees danger and hides himself") → 22:5 "Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them". The prudent one's hiding is a guarding of the soul. *Nephesh* here is the self that is kept from harm, and it passes the check in that sense. Strand (f) is the only strand of §2 where the one who hides has a seat, and the seat is the thing the hiding protects.

It suspends the person: *meteōrizō*, "be held in suspense" (Luk 12:29).; What it co-exists with: "little faith" (Luk 12:28), and the Gentiles' seeking (Mat 6:32).; What displaces it: looking at birds and lilies (6:26, 28); knowing "your heavenly Father knows that you need them" (6:32); "seek first the kingdom" (6:33).; The seat is stated once, at the head: "anxious about your life [*psychē*]" (Mat 6:25; Luk 12:22). The rest of the discourse inherits it.

#### Observation 19406: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_165202_414-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T16:52:11Z
- **obs_text:** Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in": This is an oracle. It opens with God, not with the people: *"I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me … I said, “Here I am, here I am,”"* (v1); *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices"* (v2); The wrong choosing in v12 is made in front of a God who is calling and holding out his hands.; The oracle shows what they turned to instead: sacrifices *"in gardens"*, sitting *"in tombs"*, eating *"pig’s flesh"* (v3–4); a pride that says *"do not come near me, for I am too holy for you"* (v5); they *"forget my holy mountain"* and *"set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny"* (v11); They put their trust in luck and fate.; The answer turns on their own word: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12). In Hebrew, "Destiny" (Meni, H4507) and "destine" (manah, H4487) come from the same root. They poured cups for Destiny, and the Lord destines them. What they chose to trust becomes the form their judgement takes.; The verse then gives the reason, and the reason is in the inner being: *"because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."* The choosing does not stand alone. It is the far end of not answering and not listening. When they turned away from the voice calling them, that was already a choice, and choosing what God does not delight in is where it ends.; There is a phrase to set beside Joshua 24. There, the choice turned on what was *"evil in your eyes"*. Here they *"did what was evil in my eyes"*. The measure has moved from their eyes to God's, and his delight is the standard their choice is judged by.; In the same oracle the word "chosen" is used of the others: *"my chosen shall possess it"* (v9); *"You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse"* (v15); So in one passage there are those who chose what God did not delight in, and those God calls *"my chosen"*. The outcome sets the two side by side and reaches the inner being on both sides: *"my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (v14). The choice ends in the heart and spirit of the one who made it.

#### Observation 19606: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_165455_430-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T16:55:10Z
- **obs_text:** Psalm 105:43: "his chosen ones with singing": Psalm 105 is a call to remember. It is addressed to the chosen: *"Remember the wondrous works that he has done … O offspring of Abraham, his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!"* (v5–6). It starts with the heart: *"let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice!"* (v3).; The psalm's reason is God's own remembering: *"He remembers his covenant forever"* (v8); *"For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant"* (v42); The verse follows straight on: *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (v43). The joy and singing are set on the people brought out. They come with being brought out, and the bringing out comes from God remembering his promise. The chosen are told to remember (v5) because he remembered (v8, v42).; On the way there the psalm tells one man's inward testing: *"His feet were hurt with fetters … until what he had said came to pass, the word of the Lord tested him"* (v18–19). That man was Joseph, sent ahead of the chosen.; Psalm 105 tells nothing of the people's failures. It has *"none among his tribes who stumbled"* (v37). Its last verse states the purpose of the whole: *"that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws"* (v45).

#### Observation 19621: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: read; run_id: RUN-20261026_165600_610-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T16:56:20Z
- **obs_text:** Numbers 17:5: "Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel": The verse closes a long dispute over who God has chosen. It begins in Numbers 16. Korah and 250 chiefs, *"chosen from the assembly, well-known men"* (16:2; *qārîʾ*, H7148, "called"), rise up: *"Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the Lord?"* (16:3). Moses answers with God's choosing: *"The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him"* (16:5), and *"the man whom the Lord chooses shall be the holy one"* (16:7).; Moses names what is underneath the complaint: *"is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you … And would you seek the priesthood also?"* (16:9–10). What they already have is not enough. They seek more.; *"Therefore it is against the Lord that you and all your company have gathered together. What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (16:11). The grumbling at Aaron is against the Lord.; Psalm 106 names the same event with an inner word: *"When men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord, the earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram"* (Psa 106:16–17).; Moses himself is *"very angry"* (16:15). The rebels are judged (16:31–35). The next day *"all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, 'You have killed the people of the Lord'"* (16:41). A plague begins, and Aaron *"stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped"* (16:48).; Then God settles it with the staffs: *"And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you"* (17:5). The grumbling is against Moses and Aaron, and God calls it *"from me"*. In v10 it is *"their grumblings against me"*. The staff is kept *"as a sign for the rebels, that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die"* (17:10).; The grumbling turns to terror: *"Behold, we perish, we are undone, we are all undone. Everyone who comes near … shall die. Are we all to perish?"* (17:12–13).; "Grumble" is *lûn* (H3885B). The verse shows it as spoken complaint. I read the inner side from the passage: the seeking of the priesthood (16:10), and the jealousy that Psalm 106:16 names.

#### Observation 19940: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_170137_567-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T17:02:22Z
- **obs_text:** Grumbling, and seeking more. When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also?"* (Num 16:10). The grumbling at Aaron was against God: *"What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (16:11), and God calls it *"the grumblings … which they grumble against you"*, to be made to *"cease from me"* (17:5). Psalm 106 names the inner act: *"men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron"* (Psa 106:16). God's reply was to make the choice plain, with the staff that sprouted. Then the grumbling became terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (Num 17:13).

#### Observation 19956: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_170137_567-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T17:02:22Z
- **obs_text:** Seeking, and not obtaining. *"Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"* (Rom 11:7). The rest were seeking. They were given *"eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear"* (11:8). Paul at once refuses the conclusion that this is the end: *"did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!"* (11:11). The remnant is chosen *"by grace"*, not works (11:5–6). The passage says how the elect were chosen. It does not say why the rest were not.

#### Observation 19957: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_170137_567-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T17:02:22Z
- **obs_text:** An inner act weighed by what God chooses: In one passage the inner act of the others is itself set against God's choosing. The people fast and ask, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"* (Isa 58:3). They *"delight to know my ways"* and *"delight to draw near to God"* (58:2). Yet *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (58:3). Then: *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). "Humble himself" is the humbling of the soul, the same words as their own complaint. What God does choose is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7).; The self-humbling they offered was not wrong in itself. The passage says it stood beside oppression and quarrelling in the same people, and that it was not what he chooses.

#### Observation 20370: stage prior-capture, tag statement, status draft, deleted 0

- basis: stated; run_id: RUN-20261026_170950_497-PRIORCAPTURE; created_at: 2026-10-26T17:11:02Z
- **obs_text:** Jeremiah 8:3: "Death shall be preferred to life": > Q1 citation: ⚠ Check. Ch 2 *Wanting to die*: "Under judgment, death is wished for and withheld". The verse says death "shall be preferred" (H0977, Niphal: *shall be chosen*). "Wished for" softens the choosing word, and "withheld" belongs to Rev 9:6 only, not to Jer 8:3.; >; > Q2 M64: Include: corroborates and adds. Corroborates Ch 2 *Wanting to die*. New: the preference is a choosing word, and the Lord declares it as part of a judgment, after the people had loved, served and gone after other things (v2).; >; > Q3 other M-codes: M25 life/death: carried in Ch 2. M58 evil, M43 declares, M72 hosts: no.; This follows the Topheth judgment (7:30–34). The bones of kings, priests, prophets and people are brought out and spread *"before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, which they have gone after, and which they have sought and worshiped"* (8:2).; Then: *"Death shall be preferred to life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family in all the places where I have driven them"* (8:3).; "Preferred" is H0977 in the Niphal: death *shall be chosen* (literal sense of the Niphal) rather than life. The remnant prefer death, and the Lord declares it as part of the judgment.

#### Section 6: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, Breath lent, and held by God

> ## Breath lent, and held by God
> 
> Life is held in the breath, and the breath is God's to give and to take back.
> - "In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind" (Job 12:10).
> - Daniel tells a king who had praised idols that he had not honoured "the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways" (Daniel 5:23).
> - "If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust" (Job 34:14–15).
> - "When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your Spirit, they are created" (Psalm 104:29–30).
> - "No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death" (Ecclesiastes 8:8).
> - "When his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish" (Psalm 146:4). Thinking goes when the breath goes. "Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow" (Psalm 144:4), and the Lord "knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath" (Psalm 94:11).
> 
> People say the same of their own lives. "Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good" (Job 7:7). James asks, "What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes." He draws from it a way of speaking about tomorrow: "Instead you ought to say, 'If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.'" (James 4:14–15). Section 10.7 follows that.
> 
> God holds both ends. "I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "The Lord kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up" (1 Samuel 2:6). When a letter asked the king of Israel to heal a man of leprosy, he tore his clothes: "Am I God, to kill and to make alive …?" (2 Kings 5:7). And between the two ends, he keeps alive:
> - "that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine" (Psalm 33:19)
> - "He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right" (Job 36:6)
> - Joseph to his brothers: "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive" (Genesis 50:20)
> - Moses joins it to the fear of God: "to fear the Lord our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive" (Deuteronomy 6:24)
> 
> The breath does more than keep a body going. "But it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand" (Job 32:8). "The spirit of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all his innermost parts" (Proverbs 20:27). There the word the ESV renders "spirit" is *nəšāmâ* ("breath"). Words come out on it too. Job asks a friend, "With whose help have you uttered words, and whose breath has come out from you?" (Job 26:4). Not everything breathed out is good: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5). Section 10.5 follows that.
> 
> The breath can fail in a person who is still alive. After his vision Daniel says, "no strength remains in me, and no breath is left in me" (Daniel 10:17). Zion is pictured "gasping for breath, stretching out her hands" (Jeremiah 4:31). The psalm's last word gives the breath its purpose: "Let everything that has breath praise the Lord!" (Psalm 150:6).
> 
> God gives this frailty as a reason for holding back his anger: "I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made" (Isaiah 57:16). A psalm says what the holding back did, and why: "Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath. He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again" (Psalm 78:38–39). The people lived because his wrath was not stirred. And a whole life can be felt as lived under that anger: "For all our days pass away under your wrath; we bring our years to an end like a sigh" (Psalm 90:9). Chapter 13 follows this.
> 
> In this, humans and animals share one lot: "They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts" (Ecclesiastes 3:19). The flood fell on "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Genesis 6:17), and "Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died" (7:22).

#### Section 8: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, Life set before a person

> ## Life set before a person
> 
> Life is set before the inner being as something to choose. "I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live" (Deuteronomy 30:19). The same chapter also speaks of God's own work on the heart: "And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live" (30:6). The choice is made by doing, seeking and holding on:
> - "if a person does them, he shall live by them: I am the Lord" (Leviticus 18:5)
> - "Justice, and only justice, you shall follow, that you may live" (Deuteronomy 16:20)
> - "Let your heart hold fast my words; keep my commandments, and live" (Proverbs 4:4)
> - "Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight" (Proverbs 9:6)
> - "Seek me and live" (Amos 5:4); "Seek good, and not evil, that you may live" (5:14)
> - "his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4)
> 
> Long days are promised with some of the commands. "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land" (Exodus 20:12). Moses gives the law "that you may fear the Lord your God … all the days of your life, and that your days may be long" (Deuteronomy 6:2). Peter takes up a psalm: "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil" (1 Peter 3:10).
> 
> The Preacher sets another sight beside this. "There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15). And he adds: "Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God" (8:12). Scripture states both. I leave them side by side.
> 
> Death is set before a person just as plainly. "See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil" (Deuteronomy 30:15). "Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death" (Jeremiah 21:8). Proverbs marks where the other way ends:
> - "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (Proverbs 14:12)
> - "In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death" (Proverbs 12:28)
> - Wisdom: "For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the Lord, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death" (Proverbs 8:35–36). To hate wisdom is to love death.
> - "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits" (Proverbs 18:21). James calls the tongue "a restless evil, full of deadly poison" (James 3:8).
> 
> The same word can be death to one and life to another. Paul says of the message he carries: "to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?" (2 Corinthians 2:16).
> 
> Some of what kills a person is named from within. "Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple" (Job 5:2). "The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor" (Proverbs 21:25). Proverbs names more:
> - "He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray" (Proverbs 5:23)
> - "whoever hates reproof will die" (Proverbs 15:10)
> - "he who despises his ways will die" (Proverbs 19:16)
> 
> Elihu says it of those who will not hear: "if they do not listen, they perish by the sword and die without knowledge" (Job 36:12). Sections 10.1, 10.5 and 10.6 follow these.
> 
> God says what he wants. "Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?" (Ezekiel 18:23). "For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live" (18:32). He says it to people who had given up: "Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?" The answer comes at once: "turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:10–11).
> 
> The turning is a considered act, and it reaches back over the past:
> - "Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die" (Ezekiel 18:28).
> - "None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him" (18:22).
> - It reaches back the other way too: when a righteous man turns to injustice, "None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered" (18:24).
> - Trust can lean the wrong way: "if he trusts in his righteousness and does injustice, none of his righteous deeds shall be remembered, but in his injustice that he has done he shall die" (33:13).
> 
> Another's death can be laid at a person's hand. The watchman who does not warn the wicked is told, "his blood I will require at your hand"; if he warns and is not heeded, "you will have delivered your soul" (Ezekiel 33:8–9). Section 10.10 follows that.
> 
> Section 10.7 follows the choosing, and Chapter 14 the turning.
> 
> Life can also be wrongly kept or taken by words. God condemns those who were "putting to death souls who should not die and keeping alive souls who should not live, by your lying to my people, who listen to lies" (Ezekiel 13:19).

#### Section 9: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, Living before God

> ## Living before God
> 
> The opening of this chapter said that life is lived before God. Scripture shows it in an oath that people swore by life itself.
> 
> "As the Lord lives" is its commonest form, in 39 verses. In six of them a second life is joined to it, the life of the one spoken to. David to Jonathan: "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1 Samuel 20:3). Elisha, three times, to Elijah: "As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you" (2 Kings 2:2). Ittai to David: "wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be" (2 Samuel 15:21). I read the oath as placing a promise before the living God and binding the speaker to it by life.
> 
> Sometimes the oath names what God has done for the one who swears:
> - "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity" (1 Kings 1:29)
> - "As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand" (1 Kings 17:1)
> - Job, in his complaint: "As God lives, who has taken away my right, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter" (Job 27:2)
> 
> The words of the oath stay the same, but the heart that speaks them does not. David, his anger "greatly kindled", swore, "As the Lord lives, the man who has done this deserves to die" (2 Samuel 12:5). Saul swore that Jonathan should die, and the people swore back, "As the Lord lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground" (1 Samuel 14:45). Gehazi swore it on his way to take what his master had refused: "As the Lord lives, I will run after him and get something from him" (2 Kings 5:20). So the oath is judged by how it is sworn. "Though they say, 'As the Lord lives,' yet they swear falsely" (Jeremiah 5:2). It is to be sworn "in truth, in justice, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2). Section 10.5 follows the oath as speech.
> 
> God swears by his own life, and the oath carries both what he wants and what he will do. "As I live, declares the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 33:11). "As I live, declares the Lord God, I will not be inquired of by you" (Ezekiel 20:3). Paul quotes it of the end: "As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God" (Romans 14:11).
> 
> The one before whom life is lived is called "the living God". The name sets him against idols: "But the Lord is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King" (Jeremiah 10:10); "you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God" (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Habakkuk mocks the other side: "Woe to him who says to a wooden thing, Awake; to a silent stone, Arise! Can this teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in it. But the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him" (Habakkuk 2:19–20). What has no breath cannot be woken, and the one who calls on it "trusts in his own creation" (2:18). Before the living God, the answer is silence.
> 
> The inner being turns toward him, or away from him:
> - "My soul thirsts for God, for the living God" (Psalm 42:2)
> - "my heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God" (Psalm 84:2)
> - "lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God" (Hebrews 3:12)
> - "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God" (Hebrews 10:31)
> 
> His life is praised as well as sworn by: "The Lord lives, and blessed be my rock" (2 Samuel 22:47). Section 10.9 follows this.
> 
> Scripture counts a life in days, and says what the days are for. Israel was gathered "so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so" (Deuteronomy 4:10). The king "shall read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the Lord his God" (17:19). The Passover was kept "that all the days of your life you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt" (16:3). The psalmists give the length of their lives to praise: "I will praise the Lord as long as I live" (Psalm 146:2); "that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life" (Psalm 27:4). And a life can be summed at its end. Jacob said to Pharaoh, "Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life" (Genesis 47:9). Sections 10.2, 10.3 and 10.9 follow these.
> 
> The world where life is lived has its own name, "the land of the living". There the goodness of God is looked for: "I believe that I shall look upon the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living!" (Psalm 27:13); "You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living" (Psalm 142:5). Hezekiah, told he would die, mourned that he would leave it: "I shall not see the Lord, the Lord in the land of the living" (Isaiah 38:11). Abigail says to David that his life "shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the Lord your God" (1 Samuel 25:29).

#### Section 12: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, Death and sin

> ### Death and sin
> 
> Scripture ties death to sin from the first command. "of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die" (Genesis 2:17). The woman repeats it with more than was said: "neither shall you touch it, lest you die" (Genesis 3:3). The first word spoken against that command denies the death: "But the serpent said to the woman, 'You will not surely die.'" (Genesis 3:4).
> 
> Paul traces death's entry the same way: "just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). He names what death is in relation to sin:
> - a reign: "death reigned from Adam to Moses" (Romans 5:14)
> - a wage: "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23)
> - a sting: "The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law" (1 Corinthians 15:56)
> 
> He sets another reign against it: "as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life" (Romans 5:21).
> 
> James and Paul describe the movement from within, in their own order. James: "Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death" (James 1:15). Paul: "our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death" (Romans 7:5); "I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:9); "The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me" (Romans 7:10). Section 10.6 follows the desire, and Chapter 12 the sin.
> 
> These verses do not always say which death they mean. "The wages of sin is death" is set against "eternal life" (Romans 6:23). "Sin when it is fully grown brings forth death" (James 1:15). "If you live according to the flesh you will die" (Romans 8:13). "The soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4). I read Romans 6:23, where the opposite is eternal life, as speaking of more than the body's death. The others I leave as they are written.
> 
> In Acts a lie is followed at once by death. Peter asks Ananias, "Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God." "When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it" (Acts 5:4–5). His wife dies the same way (5:10).
> 
> Each person answers for his own. "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4). "But each one shall die for his own sin" (2 Kings 14:6; from Deuteronomy 24:16). Jeremiah repeats it: "everyone shall die for his own iniquity" (Jeremiah 31:30). Jesus says it of unbelief: "unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins" (John 8:24). John speaks of "sin that leads to death" and of sin that does not, and tells a believer to ask life for a brother whose sin does not lead to death (1 John 5:16–17). He does not say which sin leads to death, and I do not guess.
> 
> Sin can be put away while a death still follows. Nathan says to David, "The Lord also has put away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the Lord, the child who is born to you shall die" (2 Samuel 12:13–14).

#### Section 18: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, Soul, spirit and heart at death

> ## Soul, spirit and heart at death
> 
> At death Scripture speaks of each inner word in its own way. For the soul, it has more than one way.
> 
> **The soul.**
> - **It departs.** "As her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni" (Genesis 35:18).
> - **It dies.** Balaam: "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). Samson: "Let me die with the Philistines" (Judges 16:30). In both, the Hebrew is *let my soul die*. And "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4).
> - **It is poured out.** Of the servant: "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12). Before his death Jesus said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38).
> - **It is named to the very end.** Even the corpse is *nephesh* ("soul"): "Whoever touches the dead body of any person" (Numbers 19:11).
> - **It has an end beyond death, and Psalm 49 names two.** The psalm is about the death that comes to everyone: "even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish" (Psalm 49:10). Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (49:19). Of himself, the psalmist says: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (49:15). The psalm does not say what being received involves, and I do not fill it in. Of those who trust in their wealth it says, "death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning" (49:14), and it draws a word for the living from this: "Be not afraid when a man becomes rich" (49:16).
> - **It is not abandoned.** David wrote, "you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption" (Psalm 16:10). Peter reads it of Christ's death and rising: "he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption" (Acts 2:31).
> 
> I read the soul in these verses as the person: the one who dies, and the one who is ransomed. It is more than a part that leaves.
> 
> **The spirit.**
> - **The spirit is committed and returns.** "Into your hand I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:5). Jesus "yielded up his spirit" (Matthew 27:50). "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!" (Luke 23:46). Stephen: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59). "The dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7).
> - **The body without it is dead.** "The body apart from the spirit is dead" (James 2:26).
> - **Where it goes, the Preacher leaves as a question:** "Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). I leave it where he left it.
> 
> No verse sends the soul one way and the spirit another. Of the verses that name Sheol or Hades, some speak of the soul and none speaks of the spirit.
> 
> **The heart.**
> - **It stops attending.** When the wife of Phinehas heard that the ark was taken and her husband dead, the women told her, "Do not be afraid, for you have borne a son". "But she did not answer or pay attention" (1 Samuel 4:20). Literally, she did not *set her heart*. Rachel is told almost the same words, "Do not fear, for you have another son" (Genesis 35:17).
> 
> And one thing I did not expect: **the heart can die before the body does**. When Nabal sobered up and heard how close he had come to disaster, "his heart died within him, and he became as a stone. And about ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died" (1 Samuel 25:37–38). The heart died first; the man died ten days later. The psalmist knows a similar death in life: "I have been forgotten like one who is dead; I have become like a broken vessel" (Psalm 31:12). Literally, forgotten *from the heart*.
> 
> Scripture speaks of the heart while a person lives: "madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead" (Ecclesiastes 9:3). I have found no verse that speaks of the heart after death.

#### Section 23: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, The body raised

> ## The body raised
> 
> The hope Scripture gives does not leave the body behind. Job says it of his own flesh: "For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth. And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God, whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. My heart faints within me!" (Job 19:25–27). The psalmist says it of waking: "As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness" (Psalm 17:15).
> - "Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! … the earth will give birth to the dead" (Isaiah 26:19).
> - A few verses earlier, of other lords: "They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise" (26:14).
> 
> Paul ties the raising of the body to the Spirit already living within: "If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you" (Romans 8:11). The body's raising is still to come. But Paul also speaks of believers as raised already: they were "raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God" (Colossians 2:12), and God "raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 2:6). He draws from it at once where the mind is to be: "If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth" (Colossians 3:1–2). He prays that they may know "the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe", the power "that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead" (Ephesians 1:19–20). Peter says the same of new birth. God "has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3), "not of perishable seed but of imperishable" (1:23), "so that your faith and hope are in God" (1:21). Chapter 14 follows that.

#### Section 29: chapter 02 Life, breath and death, After death

> ## After death
> 
> Scripture does speak of people alive before God after death, and it uses both words.
> - John sees "under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God", crying out for justice (Revelation 6:9–10).
> - Hebrews speaks of "the spirits of the righteous made perfect" (Hebrews 12:23).
> - Peter speaks of "the spirits in prison" (1 Peter 3:19).
> - And Jesus: "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28).
> 
> Whether soul or spirit is used, these verses speak of people alive before God after death.
> 
> Other verses say that the dead are silent and gone:
> - "But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he?" (Job 14:10)
> - "As the cloud fades and vanishes, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come up; he returns no more to his house, nor does his place know him anymore" (Job 7:9–10)
> - "For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten" (Ecclesiastes 9:5). The Preacher draws the living back to the work in hand: "Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, to which you are going" (9:10).
> - "For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?" (Psalm 6:5)
> - "The dead do not praise the Lord, nor do any who go down into silence" (Psalm 115:17)
> - "Do you work wonders for the dead? Do the departed rise up to praise you?" (Psalm 88:10)
> - "For Sheol does not thank you; death does not praise you; those who go down to the pit do not hope for your faithfulness. The living, the living, he thanks you, as I do this day" (Isaiah 38:18–19)
> - Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (Psalm 49:19)
> 
> Other passages speak of the dead in Sheol as stirred and speaking. They are oracles against kings and nations.
> - In the taunt against the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4): "Sheol beneath is stirred up to meet you when you come; it rouses the shades to greet you, all who were leaders of the earth". They say to him, "You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us!" (14:9–10).
> - Over Egypt: "The mighty chiefs shall speak of them, with their helpers, out of the midst of Sheol: 'They have come down, they lie still, the uncircumcised, slain by the sword.'" Those who "spread terror in the land of the living" now "bear their shame with those who go down to the pit" (Ezekiel 32:21, 24). The trees of Eden "were comforted in the world below" at Pharaoh's fall (31:16), and Pharaoh "will be comforted for all his multitude" (32:31).
> 
> These are prophetic oracles. Jesus also tells of two men after death, and the one who is buried is aware and speaks:
> - "The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side" (Luke 16:22–23).
> - He cries, "I am in anguish in this flame". Abraham answers, "Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things … but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish", and "between us and you a great chasm has been fixed" (16:24–26).
> - He asks for his five brothers, and is told, "If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead" (16:28–31).
> 
> In this account the dead remember, see, ask and are answered. One is comforted and one is in anguish, and the line between them cannot be crossed. The account does not say whether it is a story Jesus tells or an event, and I do not decide it.
> 
> So Scripture speaks of the dead in more than one way. Some verses say they know nothing, do not praise and do not return. The oracles and Luke 16 speak of them as stirred and speaking, comforted or in anguish. I do not make one of these explain the other away.
> 
> And with God, the dead are carried, blessed and at rest:
> - "The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side" (Luke 16:22), where "now he is comforted" (16:25)
> - "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on." "Blessed indeed," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!" (Revelation 14:13)
> - David, of his dead child: "I shall go to him, but he will not return to me" (2 Samuel 12:23)
> - Jesus, answering a question about the resurrection: "Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him" (Luke 20:38)
> - "who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him" (1 Thessalonians 5:10)
> - The psalmist: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (Psalm 49:15)
> - To the man dying beside him: "Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43)
> - Paul, weighing life and death: "My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account" (Philippians 1:23–24)
> - "we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). In the same chapter he says, "not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed" (5:4, in "Waited for", above). Both are stated
> - Peter: "the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does" (1 Peter 4:6)
> 
> Scripture states both. I leave them side by side.
> 
> The living are told how to deal with the dead. Inquiring of them is forbidden: there shall not be found among you "a necromancer or one who inquires of the dead" (Deuteronomy 18:11). Israel is condemned because they "ate sacrifices offered to the dead" (Psalm 106:28). Kindness to the dead is blessed. Naomi says to her daughters-in-law, "May the Lord deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me" (Ruth 1:8).

#### Section 50: chapter 04 The heart, The heart is hidden, and God sees it

> ## The heart is hidden, and God sees it
> 
> "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9). "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy" (Proverbs 14:10). Other people cannot fully see into it, and often its owner cannot either. But "man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). The word corrects a prophet. Samuel had looked on Eliab and "thought, 'Surely the Lord's anointed is before him'" (16:6). The one sent to choose formed his thought from what he saw. God is the one who "knows the secrets of the heart" (Psalm 44:21). "You discern my thoughts from afar" (Psalm 139:2). He knows the heart's leaning before it acts: "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21). He tests it and weighs it: "the Lord weighs the heart" (Proverbs 21:2). People try to hide what the heart holds, and Isaiah answers them: "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?' You turn things upside down!" (Isaiah 29:15–16). Section 10.11 follows hiding and disclosing.
> 
> The heart can lead a person away from life itself. "Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God" (Hebrews 3:12). Paul traces being "alienated from the life of God" to "the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18). Chapter 2 ("Living before God", "Death in the living") gives the setting.
> 
> The heart is tied to life and death in plain words. "The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense" (Proverbs 10:21). The word for "sense" there is *heart*.
