"Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?" (Ezekiel 18:31). And what is believed in the heart is that God raised Jesus "from the dead" (Romans 10:9). Of the heart after death, I have found nothing (Chapter 2, "Soul, spirit and heart at death").

#### Section 122: chapter 10.2 Knowing and hearing, (opening)

> # 10.2 Knowing and hearing
> 
> Knowing belongs chiefly to the heart, as Chapter 4 showed. To pay attention is to set the heart. To understand is to have a *hearing heart*. To remember is to keep a thing in the heart. The spirit knows the self from within: "who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him?" (1 Corinthians 2:11). The soul receives what is known as something good to taste: "knowledge will be pleasant to your soul" (Proverbs 2:10).
> 
> **Hearing is the main way in.** The ear receives, and the heart keeps it or refuses it. "All my words that I shall speak to you receive in your heart, and hear with your ears" (Ezekiel 3:10). "Making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding" (Proverbs 2:2). When the heart is hard, hearing stops: "Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen" (Exodus 7:13). "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law" (Zechariah 7:12). A crushed spirit can block hearing as well. Israel "did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery" (Exodus 6:9).
> 
> A refusal to hear can stand on a reading of the past. The survivors in Egypt told Jeremiah, "As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you" (Jeremiah 44:16). Their reason was what they remembered: "For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster. But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything" (44:17–18). They had seen the ruin (44:2; 10.13, *Seen and not taken in*) and read it the other way. I read the refusal as resting on their own account of cause and effect.
> 
> What is heard moves everything inside. Rahab says, "As soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you" (Joshua 2:11). Good news works the other way: "Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country" (Proverbs 25:25). And hearing is a kind of eating: "Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food. Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live" (Isaiah 55:2–3).
> 
> Sometimes hearing is not enough, and the inner being needs to *see*. Jacob's heart went numb at the news that Joseph was alive. His spirit revived only when he saw the wagons (Genesis 45:26–27).
> 
> Understanding has a source that Scripture names in the breath: "it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand" (Job 32:8; Chapter 2). And hearing God himself was a matter of life. "Did any people ever hear the voice of a god speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and still live?" (Deuteronomy 4:33). Section 10.9 follows this.
> 
> **Hearing goes both ways.** The ear is the way in, and it is also where what goes out arrives. God hears what people say: "You have heard their taunts, O Lord, all their plots against me" (Lamentations 3:61). "Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another. The Lord paid attention and heard them" (Malachi 3:16). And refusing to hear goes with devising. "I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words" (Jeremiah 6:19). Jeremiah's enemies plot against him with these words: "let us not pay attention to any of his words" (Jeremiah 18:18).
> 
> What a person listens to shows what he is: *"An evildoer listens to wicked lips, and a liar gives ear to a mischievous tongue"* (Proverbs 17:4).
> 
> Who speaks can decide whether a word is heard. In the Preacher's example a poor, wise man "by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man. But I say that wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard" (Ecclesiastes 9:15–16). His wisdom had saved them. I read the verse as saying that what was seen in him was his poverty, and that was why he was forgotten and not heard (10.3).
> 
> Hearing can be taken away, and then wanted. *"Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord God, when I will send a famine on the land—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord. They shall wander from sea to sea … to seek the word of the Lord, but they shall not find it. In that day the lovely virgins and the young men shall faint for thirst"* (Amos 8:11–13). The famine is not of the word but of hearing it. The bodily thirst comes in the same day.
> 
> Before Samuel, *"the word of the Lord was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision"* (1 Samuel 3:1). The word for *rare* is the word for *precious*. When the call came, the boy did not know it: *"Samuel did not yet know the Lord, and the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him"* (3:7). Three times he ran to Eli, until *"Eli perceived that the Lord was calling the boy"* and taught him the answer, *"Speak, Lord, for your servant hears"* (3:8–9). The old priest, whose eyes were growing dim (3:2), knew the voice the boy could not yet place. I read hearing that had to be learned, in a time when the word was rare.
> 
> Hearing can stop at a single word. Paul tells the crowd of his vision in the temple: *"Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me"* (Acts 22:18). He objected that they knew his past: *"Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you"* (22:19). The answer was *"Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles"* (22:21). Then *"Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, 'Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live'"* (22:22). They heard him through the persecution and the vision; the word "Gentiles" ended their hearing. Paul had thought his past would make them listen; the Lord had said it would not.
> 
> Ears can be closed to a word that is still being spoken. "To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen; behold, the word of the Lord is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it" (Jeremiah 6:10). The act is a hearing that does not happen. "Cannot listen" is followed by what they do with the word instead: they scorn it. Taking no pleasure in it is the measure of the scorn. I read the uncircumcised ears as hearing that lacks the mark of belonging to him. The one who must speak is left holding it: "Therefore I am full of the wrath of the Lord; I am weary of holding it in" (6:11).
> 
> Words that are heard can be pictured as tools. The Preacher *"sought to find words of delight, and uprightly he wrote words of truth"* (Ecclesiastes 12:10). *"The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd. My son, beware of anything beyond these"* (12:11–12). A goad drives an animal on; a nail holds something in place. I read the figure as two works of the same words on the hearer: they move him, and they fix in him. Delight is in the search for the words, and the words are given by one Shepherd.
> 
> What is heard can also kindle. "I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words" (Nehemiah 5:6). And when what is heard lowers the hearers' standing or exposes their guilt, rage can refuse to hear any more. Stephen's hearers "were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him … But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him" (Acts 7:54, 57). James puts hearing first for this very reason: "let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (James 1:19–20).
> 
> The same words, read aloud, brought fear to some and none to others. When the scroll of Jeremiah's words was read, the officials "heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king cut it up column by column and burned it, and "neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments" (36:23–24).
> 
> Understanding can itself be dread: "it will be sheer terror to understand the message" (Isaiah 28:19; Chapter 13). And some hold the word in awe: "Princes persecute me without cause, but my heart stands in awe of your words" (Psalm 119:161). Section 10.9 follows those who tremble at his word.
> 
> Some things are only understood later. Of God's anger, Jeremiah says, "In the latter days you will understand it clearly" (Jeremiah 23:20). Chapter 13 follows how people read, and misread, what has happened to them.
> 
> God also says what knowing him is. Of Josiah: "He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the Lord" (Jeremiah 22:16). It is said against his son, who built "by unrighteousness" and kept back his neighbour's wages (22:13): "But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence" (22:17). Knowing God is named here in a deed done for the poor, and set against a heart and eyes given to gain (10.6).
> 
> Knowing has a beginning, and Scripture names it. "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction" (Proverbs 1:7). "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" (Proverbs 9:10; Psalm 111:10). To man God said, "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding" (Job 28:28). It also runs the other way. The one who seeks wisdom "as for hidden treasures" is told, "then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God" (Proverbs 2:4–5). And it can be refused: "Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the Lord" (Proverbs 1:29). The fear of God is also learned by hearing (10.9).
> 
> Learning to fear God takes a life. Israel was gathered "so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so" (Deuteronomy 4:10). The ear decides much: "The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise" (Proverbs 15:31). God can open the ear himself. In a dream "he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings, that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man" (Job 33:16–17). Chapter 2 ("Living before God", "Delivered from death") gives the setting.
> 
> Wisdom, refused, says: "I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you" (Proverbs 1:26). And "whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster" (1:33).
> 
> What is known is also kept and returned to. Remembering feeds thinking: "I remember the days of old; I meditate on all that you have done; I ponder the work of your hands" (Psalm 143:5).
> 
> Hearing can be woken. "The Lord God has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught. The Lord God has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward" (Isaiah 50:4–5). The order is the verses' own: the ear is woken before the tongue sustains anyone, and it is woken each morning. The next verse goes on to "I gave my back to those who strike" (50:6), so the woken ear is no shelter from suffering. An angel wakes a prophet too, and the first thing said is "What do you see?" (Zechariah 4:1–2; 13.2).
> 
> What is known can be known in heart and soul. Joshua, near death: "you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the Lord your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed" (Joshua 23:14). This is knowing from experience. He turns it into a warning straight away: "But just as all the good things that the Lord your God promised concerning you have been fulfilled for you, so the Lord will bring upon you all the evil things" (23:15). The faithfulness they know from the good is the same faithfulness that stands behind the warnings.
> 
> Receiving a word can wait on being willing. "and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (Matthew 11:14–15). The Bereans "received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed" (Acts 17:11–12). Paul calls a saying "trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost" (1 Timothy 1:15). The other way is also named: scoffers "following their own sinful desires … deliberately overlook this fact" (2 Peter 3:3, 5). I read the willing, or the unwilling, as standing before the hearing in these verses.

#### Section 144: chapter 10.4 Thinking, Small, passing, and wholly seen

> ## Small, passing, and wholly seen
> 
> Human thought is real, and it is also small. "The Lord — knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath" (Psalm 94:11).
> 
> And none of it is hidden.
> - "You discern my thoughts from afar" (Psalm 139:2).
> - "The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9).
> - He knows the inclination before it is acted on: "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21).
> - Jesus "perceived their thoughts" (Luke 5:22).
> - What is hidden will be brought out. Simeon says the child is set for a sign "so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed" (Luke 2:34–35).
> 
> The same psalm that says God knows my thoughts uses the same word for his thoughts: "How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!" (Psalm 139:17).
> 
> God thinks too, and his thinking is not like mine. "The Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). In the plea that Joab put in a woman's mouth to move David (2 Samuel 14:3), she says of God that "he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14). "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isaiah 55:8). Chapter 11 returns to this.

#### Section 189: chapter 10.7 Choosing and setting direction, Others around a choice

> ## Others around a choice
> 
> A choice does not stay between the one who chooses and the one chosen. Others stand near it: at the place God chose, turned toward it from far away, set against the person chosen, standing with them, or knowing that a choice was made. The verses seldom say what these others feel about the choosing itself. They say what they are to do and be around it, and what moves them.
> 
> **At the place God chose.** When God chooses a place, the people are not told to admire it. They are told what to be there. They are to rejoice: *"you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you undertake"* (Deuteronomy 12:18). The joy rests on the blessing, not on the place: *"in which the Lord your God has blessed you"* (12:7). At the Feast of Booths the joy is what the blessing is for: *"because the Lord your God will bless you … so that you will be altogether joyful"* (16:15). The joy is never had alone. The servants, the Levite, *"the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow"* are named in it (16:11), and the one rejoicing is told in the next breath, *"You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt"* (16:12).
> 
> Fear is learned there too, at a meal: *"that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always"* (Deuteronomy 14:23). In the same passage the people spend their money *"for whatever you desire … whatever your appetite craves"*, and *"eat there before the Lord your God and rejoice"* (14:26). Fear of the Lord, a satisfied appetite and joy belong to the one meal, and the passage does not set them against each other. When a case is *"too difficult for you"*, the decision is sought at the place, and what is asked is *"you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"* (17:8, 10). Presumption is the opposite, and its end is that *"all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again"* (17:13). I read this as a person's own judgement reaching its limit and being asked to yield. The passage names the limit and the carefulness, not the struggle.
> 
> **Desire, near and far.** The soul's desire comes in twice, turned two ways. Away from the place it is given room. If the place is too far, *"you may eat within your towns whenever you desire"* (Deuteronomy 12:21). In the same words, desire draws a man to the place: a Levite *"may come when he desires"*, literally with all the desire of his soul, *"to the place that the Lord will choose"* (18:6). His coming is left to that desire. It is the account of wanting (10.6) seen from beside a choice.
> 
> **Turned toward it from far off.** For people far from the chosen city, the city is the direction of their prayer. Solomon's prayer takes the hardest case: the people in captivity because they sinned, *"for there is no one who does not sin"* (1 Kings 8:46). The turning happens in the enemy's land, in steps. First *"if they turn their heart"*, then words, *"We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly"* (8:47), then *"if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul … and pray to you toward … the city that you have chosen"* (8:48). "Turn" and "repent" are the one verb. Solomon prays it to the one who alone knows hearts (8:39), and he asks God himself to *"incline our hearts to him"* (8:58). Nehemiah prays from exile in the same verb, holding God to his word: *"if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, … I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen"* (Nehemiah 1:9). The return is to God, and the place is where he brings those who return.
> 
> **Set against the one chosen.** Several passages show others turning on someone chosen, and each names what moves them.
> - **Grumbling, and seeking more.** When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also? … What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (Numbers 16:10–11). Psalm 106 calls it jealousy (106:16). God counts the grumbling as against himself, and makes his choice plain *"to cease from me the grumblings"* (Numbers 17:5). Once it was plain, the grumbling turned to terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (17:13).
> - **Anger at what a choice costs.** Saul's anger is kindled against Jonathan: *"do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame"* (1 Samuel 20:30). He gives his reason: *"neither you nor your kingdom shall be established"* (20:31). The anger is for his house, and it ends in a spear thrown at his own son (20:33). Jonathan chose in love, *"for he loved him as he loved his own soul"* (20:17). His anger in reply is grief for the one he chose: *"he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him"* (20:34). He keeps the choice, and seals it with an oath in the name of the Lord (20:42).
> - **Contempt in the heart.** Michal *"saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart"* (2 Samuel 6:16). It was inward before it was spoken, and when it came out its measure was the servants' eyes (6:20).
> - **Despised and abhorred.** The servant is addressed as *"one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation"* (Isaiah 49:7), in the same verb as Michal's. The same verse turns it round, not by anything the servant does: *"Kings shall see and arise … because of the Lord, who is faithful, … who has chosen you"*.
> - **A verdict drawn from ruin.** People looked at the chosen in their ruin and said *"The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose"*, and so *"despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight"* (Jeremiah 33:24).
> - **Hatred.** *"because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you"* (John 15:19). The world loves *"its own"*. The verse names the choosing as the cause. The passage says the hatred fell first on Jesus (15:18), and puts under it *"because they do not know him who sent me"* (15:21).
> - **Rejection after testing.** *"a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious"* (1 Peter 2:4).
> 
> **With the chosen, and for them.** Others stand with the chosen too. The psalmist asks to be let in: *"Remember me, O Lord, … that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"* (Psalm 106:4–5). He asks God, not the chosen, and he asks it confessing his sin (106:6). Paul writes in chains: *"I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation"* (2 Timothy 2:10). The elder loves the elect lady *"in truth"*, *"because of the truth that abides in us"* (2 John 1–2): the love rests on the truth, not on her being chosen. And whoever believes in the stone God chose *"will not be put to shame"* (1 Peter 2:6). For those who do not believe, the same stone is *"a stone of stumbling"* (2:8).
> 
> **Knowing that a choice was made, and not knowing.** Knowing of a choice can settle a quarrel. In the dispute at Jerusalem, Peter appeals to what they all know: *"you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (Acts 15:7). The purpose of God's choosing one man lay in others, that they would hear and believe, and their hearts were *"cleansed … by faith"* (15:9). The debate falls silent (15:12). Paul knows that the Thessalonians are chosen from what he saw happen: *"because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5).
> 
> Not knowing does not stop God from using a man for the sake of the chosen. To Cyrus: *"For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me"* (Isaiah 45:4). Knowing is still held out to him: *"that you may know that it is I"* (45:3). Of those outside the chosen, Paul says *"Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"* (Romans 11:7). They were seeking, and did not see. He refuses at once to make it the end: *"did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!"* (11:11).
> 
> **An inner act weighed by what God chooses.** In one passage what the others offer from within is set against God's own choosing. The people fast and complain, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"*, while *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (Isaiah 58:3). God answers, *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). What he chooses is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7). The humbling stood beside oppression in the same people, and it was not what he chooses. The same people *"delight to know my ways"* (58:2), in the same delight word as Isaiah 66:4 in *Whose measure*.
> 
> The same passage opens on what they appear to be doing: "Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness and did not forsake the judgment of their God; they ask of me righteous judgments; they delight to draw near to God" (Isaiah 58:2). The act is seeking and drawing near. Their delight measures how eager it is, and "as if" says what it lacks. I read that eagerness to draw near can sit beside oppressing workers (58:3) without the person seeing the two together.
> 
> Malachi has the same pairing of seeking and delight, and God answers it. The people had said, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and he delights in them", and asked, "Where is the God of justice?" (Malachi 2:17). The answer takes their own words: "And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming" (3:1). Then: "But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire" (3:2). Their seeking and their delight are taken at their word, and the question turns back on them. I read a delight in what is asked for that has not yet faced what it asks. The comparison with Isaiah 58:2 is mine; each passage says its own part. His coming as refiner is in 13.1 (*Delight*).
> 
> **Rule offered, refused, and sought.** "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." Gideon refused: "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the Lord will rule over you" (Judges 8:22–23). Daniel, offered a place as third ruler for reading the writing, refused the reward and did the task: "Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king and make known to him the interpretation" (Daniel 5:17). Gideon's son sought what his father refused, and won it by kinship. "Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you? Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh." And "their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'" (Judges 9:2–3). He then killed his seventy brothers (9:5). The verses set refusing and seeking side by side in one family, and say no more about why.

#### Section 194: chapter 10.7 Choosing and setting direction, Setting the heart

> ## Setting the heart
> 
> The choice at Shechem is spoken with the mouth, and Joshua does not take it as the whole. He calls at once for the heart: *"Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the Lord"* (Joshua 24:23). The people had just chosen the Lord, and the foreign gods were still among them. Samuel says it in nearly the same words: *"put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the Lord and serve him only"* (1 Samuel 7:3). In both, putting something away goes with turning the heart.
> 
> Scripture speaks of the heart being set, inclined and directed, and of the state it is in:
> - **Inclined, and asked for.** *"Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain!"* (Psalm 119:36). The one who prays this has just chosen (119:30), and asks God to do the inclining.
> - **Whole or divided.** *"unite my heart to fear your name"* (Psalm 86:11), against *"a double heart"* (Psalm 12:2). Solomon's *"heart was not wholly true to the Lord his God"* (1 Kings 11:4).
> - **Stubborn.** *"the stubbornness of their evil hearts"* runs through Jeremiah (Jeremiah 7:24).
> - **Moved from within.** *"everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him"* (Exodus 35:21) puts heart and spirit side by side in setting out to give.
> - **Set, beside a wrong love.** Jehoshaphat was told, *"Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you from the Lord. Nevertheless, some good is found in you, for you destroyed the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God"* (2 Chronicles 19:2–3). A love wrongly given and a heart set to seek God stand in one king, and the prophet's verdict holds both.
> - **Set to study, to do and to teach.** *"For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the Lord, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel"* (Ezra 7:10). The setting has three steps, and the doing stands between the study and the teaching. The verse before ends *"for the good hand of his God was on him"* (7:9), and this one opens with *"For"*. I read the second *"For"* as giving the good hand its ground in Ezra's heart. Its opposite is Rehoboam, who *"did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord"* (2 Chronicles 12:14; 10.14).
> - **Set as an aim.** The word for ambition is used three times by Paul, and its aims are not what ambition usually seeks: *"I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named"* (Romans 15:20); *"whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ"* (2 Corinthians 5:9–10); *"aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands"* (1 Thessalonians 4:11). Also: *"If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task"* (1 Timothy 3:1). I read the aims as going where no one has gone, pleasing him wherever one is, and quietness.
> 
> The heart's leaning is prayed against, and a rebuke is welcomed. "Do not let my heart incline to any evil, to busy myself with wicked deeds in company with men who work iniquity, and let me not eat of their delicacies! Let a righteous man strike me—it is a kindness; let him rebuke me—it is oil for my head; let my head not refuse it" (Psalm 141:4–5). The act is a prayer that the heart not lean, and a choice of the hard word over the sweet food. What he calls pleasant is his own words, to be heard when the judges fall: "then they shall hear my words, for they are pleasant" (141:6). The prayer ends, "But my eyes are toward you, O God, my Lord" (141:8).

#### Section 196: chapter 10.7 Choosing and setting direction, Planning

> ## Planning
> 
> A choice settles a direction. A plan carries it ahead, into a time that has not yet come. Scripture gives the inner being this power plainly. Of the builders at Babel God says, *"this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them"* (Genesis 11:6). The words for it are the words for thinking: to devise, to reckon, to purpose (10.4). They are used for a woman buying a field, a king counting his soldiers, a sailor looking for a beach, and a man plotting on his bed. This section is about the looking ahead itself. Plans made against another person are in 10.10. The next section, *Willing*, is about how a person answers what others put forward. The two often appear in the same passage.
> 
> The place of it is the heart: *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). In that one verse the plan is the person's own, and the steps are not. I read the rest of what the verses say about planning inside that verse.
> 
> **Weighing first.** Jesus asks his hearers to look ahead before they begin. "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28). A builder who lays a foundation and cannot finish is mocked: *"This man began to build and was not able to finish"* (Luke 14:30). *"Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?"* (14:31). If the answer is no, he sends for terms *"while the other is yet a great way off"* (14:32). The looking ahead here is honest about strength, and it acts early, while there is still time. Jesus uses it for following him: *"So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple"* (14:33).
> 
> The same weighing is praised in an ordinary life. The woman of Proverbs 31 *"rises while it is yet night"* (31:15). *"She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard"* (31:16). The verb for considering is a planning verb. She weighs it, and then she acts.
> 
> When something has happened that no one has seen before, the first call is to weigh it before acting. After the outrage at Gibeah, *"all who saw it said, 'Such a thing has never happened or been seen … consider it, take counsel, and speak'"* (Judges 19:30).
> 
> **Planning without knowing.** The fullest picture of planning ahead in these verses is a voyage. Paul warned the crew: *"I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss"* (Acts 27:10). They listened to the pilot and the owner instead (27:11). The plan that followed is worded with all its uncertainty:
> - *"the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix"* (27:12)
> - *"Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor"* (27:13)
> - after the storm, *"they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore"* (27:39)
> 
> *"on the chance that somehow"*, *"supposing"*, *"if possible"*: Luke records the planners' own sense that they could not see far. The first plan was undone by the wind (Acts 27:14). The last was undone by a reef they had not seen (27:41).
> 
> Paul plans the same way, and says so. *"I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented)"* (Romans 1:13). His intending was real and often repeated, and something outside him held it back. James says what such planning should sound like: *"If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that"* (James 4:15; see *Life and death set before a person*).
> 
> Paul's own plans are said under God's will, again and again, and his wanting stays strong inside them.
> - At parting: "I will return to you if God wills" (Acts 18:21), after he "declined" to stay longer (18:20).
> - With purpose: "I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power" (1 Corinthians 4:19). He then asks their will: "What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love?" (4:21).
> - With his own wish: "I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits" (16:7).
> - In prayer: "asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you. For I long to see you" (Romans 1:10–11); "so that by God's will I may come to you with joy" (15:32).
> - Hindered: "we wanted to come to you, I, Paul, again and again, but Satan hindered us" (1 Thessalonians 2:18), after "with great desire to see you face to face" (2:17).
> - Yielded by others: "since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, 'Let the will of the Lord be done'" (Acts 21:14), after "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?" (21:13).
> - A wish set beside a gift: "I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God" (1 Corinthians 7:7).
> The verses keep apart Paul's wanting, God's will, and what hinders, named once as Satan. I read the plan as held open toward God without the wanting being given up.
> 
> **A plan carries a person's word.** When Paul changed his travel plans, he was charged with being unreliable, and he answers with the inner question: *"Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say 'Yes, yes' and 'No, no' at the same time?"* (2 Corinthians 1:17). He rests his answer on God: *"As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No"* (1:18). In this passage, a plan is something said to others. When it changes, the change can be read as a divided heart.
> 
> **Planning together, and parting.** Plans are often made with others, and others may not agree.
> - Paul and Barnabas planned to revisit the churches. *"Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them"* (Acts 15:37–38). Each weighed the same past differently, and *"there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other"* (15:39).
> - Joseph of Arimathea sat in the council that sent Jesus to death, but he *"had not consented to their decision and action"* (Luke 23:51). He did not share their plan, and the next verse shows him acting on his own: *"This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus"* (23:52).
> 
> **Planning for another's good.** Darius *"planned to set him over the whole kingdom"* (Daniel 6:3), and the verse gives the reason: *"because an excellent spirit was in him"*. The plan for Daniel at once stirred others to look for a fault in him (6:4).
> 
> A plan can also be held against someone's good without anyone calling it a plot. Joab knew *"that the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (2 Samuel 14:1). He sent a wise woman of Tekoa with a staged plea, and *"put the words in her mouth"* (14:3). In it she told David that by leaving Absalom in exile he had *"planned such a thing against the people of God"* (14:13). Beside it she set God, who *"devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (14:14). David saw whose plan it was: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (14:19). Three are at work in the one passage: Joab's scheme, the king's planning, and God's devising as she declares it. The king's planning is measured against God's (13.1, *Purposing*).
> 
> **A purpose held.** Some plans are aimed at one's own life. *"You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress"* (Psalm 17:3). The psalmist has set a course for his own speech ahead of time, and he states it under God's testing. He goes on: *"My steps have held fast to your paths"* (17:5).
> - Barnabas, at Antioch, *"exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose"* (Acts 11:23). The verse says what moved him: he *"saw the grace of God"* and *"was glad"*.
> - Paul lists his *"aim in life"* among what Timothy had followed, beside *"my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness"* (2 Timothy 3:10).
> - David prays that God will keep what the people have set: *"keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you"* (1 Chronicles 29:18). He asks God to hold the purpose in place.
> - Paul uses a purpose word for where the mind is set: *"to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace"* (Romans 8:6). *"For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"* (8:7). Chapter 7 gives the flesh.
> - The verb of the same word names a mind set downward: *"their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things"* (Philippians 3:19). The next verse turns it: *"But our citizenship is in heaven"* (3:20). And the call uses the same verb: *"Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth"* (Colossians 3:2).
> - *"You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you"* (Isaiah 26:3).
> 
> **Devised from one's own heart.** A plan can begin in the self and stay there. Jeroboam set up his own feast *"in the month that he had devised from his own heart"* (1 Kings 12:33). The month was his own invention, set against the feast in Judah (12:32). Nehemiah said to the plotters, *"No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Nehemiah 6:8). The same capacity that looks ahead can make up what is not there (10.4, *Imagination that makes gods*).
> 
> **The plan and its outcome.** The verses do not let a plan secure its own end.
> - *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9).
> - *"Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us"* (Isaiah 8:10).
> - Gamaliel, of the apostles: *"if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them"* (Acts 5:38–39).
> - Of those who plot against the king: *"Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed"* (Psalm 21:11). Of a king's plans against strongholds: *"but only for a time"* (Daniel 11:24). The next verse says what he roused for it: *"he shall stir up his power and his heart"* (11:25). The heart is stirred up as a resource for war.
> - Counsel that cannot save: *"You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you … No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!"* (Isaiah 47:13–14). Many counsels weary the one who keeps them, and they give no warmth.
> - Joseph, of his brothers: *"you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good"* (Genesis 50:20). The same verb is used of both.
> 
> The verses also show that what a person intends is seen before it is done and will be shown in full. *"The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought"* (1 Chronicles 28:9). The Lord *"will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart"* (1 Corinthians 4:5). Paul draws a warning from it for himself: *"do not pronounce judgment before the time"* (4:5). He has just said, *"I do not even judge myself"* (4:3).
> 
> Joseph's counsel to Pharaoh plans against a famine he has been shown. "Let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man", gather the food of the good years "under the authority of Pharaoh", and keep it as "a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine", "so that the land may not perish" (Genesis 41:33–36). "This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants" (41:37).
> 

#### Section 212: chapter 10.9 Relating to God, Waiting, and pleading

> ## Waiting, and pleading
> 
> The soul can speak its hope to itself: "'The Lord is my portion,' says my soul, 'therefore I will hope in him.' The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him. It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord" (Lamentations 3:24–26). "Portion" is the word of Psalm 16:5 (10.6). Twice "good" belongs to waiting: the Lord is good to those who wait, and it is good to wait. I read waiting as the place where the soul's hope is put.
> 
> A plea can bring one's own record. Hezekiah, told he would die, "turned his face to the wall and prayed": "Please, O Lord, remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight." And he wept bitterly (Isaiah 38:2–3; 2 Kings 20:2–3). The answer came: "I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life" (Isaiah 38:5). He brought his record. God named his prayer and his tears. I note what the answer names and go no further. Chapter 2 ("Life asked for") has what he wrote afterwards.
> 
> A cry can come only in distress. Of the godless: "Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him? Will he take delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?" (Job 27:9–10). The act asked about is calling on God. I read the questions as setting a cry in distress against calling at all times. Delight in him is named as what would make the difference.
> 
> A plea can end in asking that one's work should last. The prayer of Moses that counts how short a life is (Psalm 90:10, 12) ends: "Return, O Lord! How long? Have pity on your servants!" (Psalm 90:13), "Make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us" (90:15), "Let your work be shown to your servants" (90:16), and "Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands!" (90:17). "Favor" is the word for pleasantness. What they ask to last is their own work, and they ask it under his favor, beside "your work".
> 
> A plea can come from the poor man's own mouth, and be heard. "I sought the Lord, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears … This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him and saved him out of all his troubles" (Psalm 34:4, 6). "But I am afflicted and in pain; let your salvation, O God, set me on high! … For the Lord hears the needy" (Psalm 69:29, 33). The one who calls himself poor is the one who cries, and what he is delivered from includes his fears (10.12).
> 
> A plea can be put to his will alone. "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean" (Matthew 8:2). The man does not doubt the power. He asks the will, and the will answers: "I will; be clean" (8:3; Mark 1:40–41; 13.1).

#### Section 224: chapter 10.10 Relating to others, Fear that arrives with a person

> ### Fear that arrives with a person
> 
> A person's coming can bring fear, because of what it might mean. When Samuel came to Bethlehem, "the elders of the city came to meet him trembling and said, 'Do you come peaceably?'" (1 Samuel 16:4). Ahimelech "came to meet David, trembling", and asked, "Why are you alone, and no one with you?" (1 Samuel 21:1). The question each asks shows what they feared.
> 
> Some people carry fear with them because of their power. Of Nebuchadnezzar: "because of the greatness that he gave him, all peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him. Whom he would, he killed" (Daniel 5:19). The fear followed the power over life and death, and the verse says that power was given by God. Fear can fall on a crowd because of one person: officials "helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them" (Esther 9:3).
> 
> And refusing to be afraid can provoke. When Haman saw Mordecai, "that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai" (Esther 5:9). The man who would not tremble became the one Haman set out to destroy (5:14).
> 
> Mastery can turn on the day it is hoped for. "on the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain the mastery over them, the reverse occurred: the Jews gained mastery over those who hated them", and "the fear of them had fallen on all peoples" (Esther 9:1–2). With no one able to stand against them, the Jews "did as they pleased to those who hated them" (9:5). Before that day, as the edict went out, "many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them" (8:17; 10.12).
> 
> Bathsheba met Adonijah, the brother who had lost the throne, with the same question. "Do you come peacefully?" He said, "Peacefully" (1 Kings 2:13; 10.6).
> 

#### Section 252: chapter 10.12 Fear, Dread laid on others

> ## Dread laid on others
> 
> Fear does not stay with single persons. It falls on peoples and on creatures. In most of these verses God lays it; in Esther no giver is named. The verses say what it led to.
> - "The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth" (Genesis 9:2).
> - "a terror from God fell upon the cities that were around them, so that they did not pursue the sons of Jacob" (Genesis 35:5).
> - "Put them in fear, O Lord! Let the nations know that they are but men!" (Psalm 9:20).
> - "that their hearts may melt, and many stumble. At all their gates I have given the glittering sword" (Ezekiel 21:15). The melting heart is what the sword is given for (*Fear in the body*, above).
> 
> The same dread came to different peoples and ended in different ways.
> - **Rahab:** "as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the Lord your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath" (Joshua 2:11).
> - **Moab:** "Moab was in great dread of the people, because they were many", and Balak sent for Balaam: "Come now, curse this people for me, since they are too mighty for me" (Numbers 22:3, 6).
> - **The peoples in Esther's day:** where the king's second edict reached, "there was gladness and joy among the Jews … And many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them" (Esther 8:17). The verse gives fear as the only reason. This dread did not send the peoples away, nor set them against the Jews; it brought many of them over to the name of those they feared. On the day itself, "no one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all peoples" (9:2; 10.10).
> 
> A people can itself be made a horror to others. "I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse" (Jeremiah 24:9). "Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its wounds" (Jeremiah 19:8). The feeling is in those who pass by. The verses give the reasons in the people's own deeds: "The Lord could no longer bear your evil deeds" (Jeremiah 44:22). The same root, held by the prophet, is his own grief for them: "dismay has taken hold on me" (Jeremiah 8:21).
> 
> One phrase passes through many mouths. Jeremiah gave it as a name: "The Lord does not call your name Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side" (Jeremiah 20:3). Then he heard it whispered against himself: "For I hear many whispering. Terror is on every side! 'Denounce him! Let us denounce him!' say all my close friends" (20:10). He answered: "But the Lord is with me as a dread warrior" (20:11). A psalmist heard "the whispering of many" and "terror on every side" (Psalm 31:13), and answered in his own words: "But I trust in you, O Lord; I say, 'You are my God'" (31:14).
> 
> Job's friends say that terrors chase the wicked: "Terrors frighten him on every side, and chase him at his heels" (Job 18:11). They say it of Job. God's own verdict stands over them: "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7).

#### Section 254: chapter 10.12 Fear, What changes it

> ## What changes it
> 
> The verses show fear changing character, and they point to what changes it.
> - **What it is turned toward.** At the sea Israel "feared greatly" as Egypt marched, and after the crossing "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (Exodus 14:10, 31). In between, fear spoke as a preference: "it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness" (14:12; 10.6, *Shaped by fear*). In the boat, fear of the storm became fear of the one who stilled it (Mark 4:41). In these cases the change came after God acted.
> - **One fear set in place of another, by the same speaker.** "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you" (Exodus 20:20). "do not fear what they fear … Let him be your fear" (Isaiah 8:12–13). "Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell", and then, "Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows" (Matthew 10:28, 31).
> - **Who speaks to it, and why.** God's "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10), and Jael's "do not be afraid" (Judges 4:18).
> - **Knowing whose hand is on one.** Ezra: "I took courage, for the hand of the Lord my God was on me, and I gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me" (Ezra 7:28). The verse names the ground of the courage, and the courage turns at once into a deed. Ezra then would not ask the king for soldiers, "since we had told the king, 'The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him'" (8:22; 10.14). What he told others did the same for them (Nehemiah 2:18; 10.10).
> - **Who meets it.** "When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers" (Proverbs 21:15). One scroll was read aloud: the officials "turned one to another in fear", and "neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid" (Jeremiah 36:16, 24). At the signs of the end, "people fainting with fear", and to the disciples, "straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near" (Luke 21:26, 28).
> - **One's own conduct.** "rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad" (Romans 13:3). "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered" (Isaiah 66:4). The same passage opens with the one God looks to, who "trembles at my word" (66:2). I read the passage as setting that trembling beside "their fears".
> - **Pride.** "So do not become proud, but fear" (Romans 11:20). "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jeremiah 49:16).
> - **Where the heart is.** Fear "taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me", against fear put "in their hearts" (Isaiah 29:13; Jeremiah 32:40).
> - **Faith, trust and love** (the section above).
> - **Joy or silence.** The women left the tomb "with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples" (Matthew 28:8). In Mark's account "they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid" (Mark 16:8). The two accounts stand side by side.
> - **The same root, rendered as another movement.** *Rāgaz*, "to tremble", is also anger and grief (Psalm 4:4; 2 Samuel 18:33). *Paḥad*, "dread", is also "thrill" (Isaiah 60:5). *Phobos*, "fear", is also "respect" (Romans 13:7).
> 
> Chapter 11 (§4) gathers what changes the character of a word across all the activities. These are fear's part in it.

#### Section 259: chapter 10.13 Anger, What it rises at

> ### What it rises at
> 
> Human anger in the verses is often set off by something perceived. Sometimes the verse names hearing or seeing; sometimes the setting gives the cause.
> - **A report:** Potiphar's anger rose on his wife's words (Genesis 39:19). It was not tested, and it was false.
> - **A sight:** "when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath" (Esther 5:9).
> - **A demand, an expectation or a slight.** Rachel demanded children, and "Jacob's anger was kindled against Rachel, and he said, 'Am I in the place of God?'" (Genesis 30:2). Naaman: "Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me" (2 Kings 5:11). Queen Vashti refused to come, and the king's "anger burned within him" (Esther 1:12).
> - **A rival's honour:** the women sang of David's ten thousands, and "Saul was very angry" (1 Samuel 18:8). The elder brother heard the music for his returned brother, "was angry and refused to go in" (Luke 15:28).
> - **A wrong done to another.** Jacob's sons were indignant "because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7). David burned at the rich man in Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12:5). Nehemiah: "I was very angry when I heard their outcry" (Nehemiah 5:6). Paul's "spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16).
> - **Good done,** where it breaks a rule: the ruler of the synagogue was "indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath" (Luke 13:14).
> - **A word that exposes.** At Nazareth, "When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath" (Luke 4:28). At Stephen's speech, "they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him" (Acts 7:57).
> - **Being outwitted through someone close.** Samson's riddle was got out of him through his wife's tears (Judges 14:15–17; 10.10). When the men of the city answered it, he said, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle" (14:18). The Spirit rushed upon him for the striking at Ashkelon, and then, "In hot anger he went back to his father's house" (14:19). "And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man" (14:20).
> - **Something within.** "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?" (James 4:1).
> 
> Whether what sets it off is true is part of the account. Potiphar acted on a lie. The officials raged at Jeremiah over a charge he denied: "It is a lie; I am not deserting" (Jeremiah 37:14). The disciples were indignant at the waste of ointment (Matthew 26:8). Mark says the indignation was first said "to themselves", then spoken, with the poor as its reason: "'Why was the ointment wasted like that? For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.' And they scolded her" (Mark 14:4–5). Jesus answered, "she has done a beautiful thing to me" (Matthew 26:10), and put the poor back in their own hands: "For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them" (Mark 14:7).
> 
> Anger can rise at a charge against one's own leadership. When Dathan and Abiram accused him of making himself a prince over them, "Moses was very angry and said to the Lord, 'Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them, and I have not harmed one of them'" (Numbers 16:15). He took the anger to the Lord. Fury can also drive authority received from others: "I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests", and "in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities" (Acts 26:10–11; 10.7).
> 
> Anger can rise at contempt for a request that rested on good done. David's men asked Nabal for "whatever you have at hand", and gave the ground: "your shepherds have been with us, and we did them no harm" (1 Samuel 25:7–8). Nabal answered, "Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse?" (25:10). David said, "Every man strap on his sword!" (25:13). I have not yet read the rest of the chapter, where Abigail meets him.
> 
> Anger can rest on a misreading and still decide. When the king came back from the garden, Haman "was falling on the couch where Esther was", begging for his life, and the king said, "Will he even assault the queen in my presence, in my own house?" (Esther 7:8). When the gallows had done its work, "the wrath of the king abated" (7:10).
> 

#### Section 282: chapter 10.13 Anger, The heart that turns, and the heart that does not

> ### The heart that turns, and the heart that does not
> 
> What happens next depends on the heart.
> 
> Josiah heard the book read and tore his clothes. The answer named his heart: "because your heart was penitent, and you humbled yourself before the Lord … I also have heard you" (2 Kings 22:19). Hezekiah's "heart was proud", and wrath came. "But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart … so that the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah" (2 Chronicles 32:25–26). The same heart provoked the anger and turned it.
> 
> Turning can be partial. Rehoboam humbled himself and was spared, "and he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord" (2 Chronicles 12:14).
> 
> Distress turns people both ways. Under the judges, "the Lord was moved to pity by their groaning" (Judges 2:18). Manasseh, "when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the Lord his God and humbled himself greatly" (2 Chronicles 33:12). Ahaz, in the same distress, became "yet more faithless" (28:22). The texts do not say why one turns and the other does not. They set the cases side by side.
> 
> Some hearts do not take the blow in. "It set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart" (Isaiah 42:25). Others make themselves unable to hear: "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … Therefore great anger came from the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 7:12).
> 
> And some cover the danger over with false peace. "You say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me'" (Jeremiah 2:35). Prophets "say continually to those who despise the word of the Lord, 'It shall be well with you'" (Jeremiah 23:17). John the Baptist meets the same thing: "do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father'" (Matthew 3:9).
> 
> Chapter 4 follows the heart in anger more fully.

#### Section 284: chapter 10.13 Anger, Shelter, and who can stand

> ### Shelter, and who can stand
> 
> Some of the time, the call is to shelter while the anger passes. "Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by" (Isaiah 26:20). That is exactly what Job had asked for: "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past" (Job 14:13). God offers his people what Job asked.
> 
> Zephaniah calls people to seek before the day comes: "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zephaniah 2:3). Those called are already humble and already doing his commands, and they are told to seek humility. The verse promises nothing beyond "perhaps", and the hiding is God's to give. What a person has leaned on is tested on that day: "Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death" (Proverbs 11:4).
> 
> At the end, the reverse: people call "to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb'" (Revelation 6:16). One shelter is in God; the other is from him. Isaiah: "Enter into the rock and hide in the dust from before the terror of the Lord, and from the splendor of his majesty" (Isaiah 2:10), "when he rises to terrify the earth" (2:19).
> 
> "Who can stand before his indignation? Who can endure the heat of his anger?" (Nahum 1:6). The next verse answers by pointing to the same God: "The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him" (1:7).
> 
> Psalm 76 asks the same question and gives the anger's purpose: "But you, you are to be feared! Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused? From the heavens you uttered judgment; the earth feared and was still, when God arose to establish judgment, to save all the humble of the earth" (Psalm 76:7–9). The anger is roused to save the humble, and the fear is the earth falling still before it (10.12).
> 
> The psalmist asks a question that joins God's anger and the fear of him: "Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you?" (Psalm 90:11). God's deeds are called awesome, and his enemies cringe before them. "How awesome are your deeds! So great is your power that your enemies come cringing to you" (Psalm 66:3). "The Lord will be awesome against them; for he will famish all the gods of the earth" (Zephaniah 2:11).

#### Section 296: chapter 11 Other sides of the inner being, 4. One word, opposite values

> ## 4. One word, opposite values
> 
> Again and again I found a single word for an inner state that is good in one place and bad in another. What decides is not the word but **what the inner being is yielding to, or holding firm against**.
> 
> - **A tender heart.** It melts before an enemy and spreads fear to others (Deuteronomy 20:8). But Josiah's heart "was penitent [tender]" before God's word, and God answered him with peace (2 Kings 22:19–20). The same softness is cowardice in one place and repentance in the other.
> - **A strong heart.** "Be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!" (Psalm 27:14). With Absalom, the same verb gives his servants the nerve to kill: "be courageous and be valiant" (2 Samuel 13:28). With Pharaoh it is hardening: "I will harden his heart" (Exodus 4:21), literally *strengthen*.
> - **A guarded heart.** "Keep your heart with all vigilance" (Proverbs 4:23). Three chapters later the same word describes the adulteress, "wily [guarded] of heart" (Proverbs 7:10).
> - **Crushing.** Crushed by an enemy, the spirit collapses (Psalm 143:3–4). Offered to God, a crushed spirit is the very sacrifice he wants: "a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17).
> - **Loving and hating one's own soul** (Chapter 5).
> - **Devising.** The same Hebrew verb describes the craftsmen who worked cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1) and those who plot. One word for planning means "discretion" (Proverbs 2:11), "evil devices" (Proverbs 12:2), and God's own purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2).
> - **Planning against.** God says, "I am … devising a plan against you. Return" (Jeremiah 18:11), and the people say, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18). The word and the "against" are the same. One plan is meant to bring people back, and the other is meant to silence the one who calls them.
> - **Purposing.** The verb for purposing (*zāmam*) is the psalmist's resolve: "I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress" (Psalm 17:3). It is the wicked man's plot: "The wicked plots against the righteous" (Psalm 37:12). It is the wise woman's weighing: "She considers a field and buys it" (Proverbs 31:16). And it is God's fixed purpose: "I have purposed; I have not relented" (Jeremiah 4:28). I read the change as following whom it is aimed at: one's own mouth, another's harm, one's own household, or a whole land.
> - **Willing.** The Hebrew word for being willing (*ʾāḇâ*) is almost always a "no". It is the guard's refusal to kill the priests (1 Samuel 22:17), David refusing the water for the men's sake (2 Samuel 23:17), Amnon refusing Tamar's plea (2 Samuel 13:14), and Israel refusing God's rest (Isaiah 30:15). God himself is "not willing to destroy" (2 Kings 8:19), and "will not be willing to forgive" the man who blesses himself in his stubbornness (Deuteronomy 29:20). The Greek word runs from Pilate "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (Mark 15:15) to God "not wishing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9). Each passage gives the reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, covenant, love, a self-blessing heart. I read the change as following what is refused, and for whose sake (10.7, *Willing*).
> - **Planning ahead.** The same looking ahead is a king's honest count of his strength (Luke 14:31) and sailors' guess "on the chance that somehow" (Acts 27:12). It is a man's "aim in life" (2 Timothy 3:10) and a plot "to put him to death" (John 11:53). I read the verses as setting the difference beside how much the planner can see. The king can count, the sailors cannot see the reef, and over all of it "the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).
> - **Reckoning.** People misreckon: "we esteemed him stricken" (Isaiah 53:4). God reckons faith "as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The law reckons in order to release (Leviticus 25:50). Love refuses to reckon at all: it "is not … resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
> - **Likening.** Comparing is how love praises ("I compare you, my love", Song of Songs 1:9), how comfort reaches out (Lamentations 2:13), and how worship ends ("who in the skies can be compared to the Lord?", Psalm 89:6). It is also how pride rises: "I will make myself like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:14).
> - **Reasoning.** The Greek word is Mary's honest pondering (Luke 1:29), the disciples' anxious circling (Mark 8:17), and a quarrel (Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 2:8).
> - **The nose.** The Hebrew word for anger, *ʾaph*, is the nostril where God breathed in life (Genesis 2:7), the face bowed in worship (2 Chronicles 7:3), and the face lifted in pride (Psalm 10:4). It can be given a ring in love (Ezekiel 16:12) or a hook for raging (2 Kings 19:28). "Long of nostrils" is patience, in God and in the wise (Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 14:29).
> - **Anger.** Jesus's anger heals (Mark 3:5). A crowd's anger stops its ears and kills (Acts 7:57–58). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26).
> - **Vexation.** It is provocation done to another (1 Samuel 1:6), suffering borne (1:16), and "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3).
> - **Provoking.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5), with the same word that tells believers to "stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24).
> - **Overflow.** One Hebrew word, *ʿebrah*, is the overflow of anger and the overflow of pride. God offers it to Job with irony: "Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him" (Job 40:11). And "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Proverbs 21:24), where the word is the same.
> - **Lifted up.** One Hebrew word names the heart that grew proud when Uzziah was strong (2 Chronicles 26:16) and Jehoshaphat's heart, "courageous in the ways of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 17:6). One family of words is God's majesty and human pride (Exodus 15:7; Jeremiah 48:29). And the boast moves: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom" (Jeremiah 9:23), "but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me" (9:24). What differs is where the height comes from, and which way it faces (10.15).
> - **Glory.** The verb that gives glory to God (Matthew 5:16) is the great city's own: she "glorified herself" (Revelation 18:7). The noun is the glory some take "in their shame" (Philippians 3:19), and two verses later the glory of the body to come, "like his glorious body" (3:21). The same word names glory taken where it does not belong and glory given (10.15).
> - **Storm.** The same storm word, *sāʿar*, is the angry king's mind ("the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled", 2 Kings 6:11) and the suffering city ("O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted", Isaiah 54:11).
> - **Denouncing.** "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8). But "Whoever says to the wicked, 'You are in the right,' will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations" (Proverbs 24:24). The word is empty when it goes against God's verdict, and it lands when it follows justice.
> - **A creed.** "Slow to anger" is used in worship, in pleading, in confession, in Jonah's complaint, in praise, in wonder, in announcing judgment, and as the ground for returning (Chapter 10.9).
> - **Mourning.** Aaron is forbidden to mourn "lest … wrath come" (Leviticus 10:6). When the wrath has come, mourning is commanded (Jeremiah 4:8).
> - **God's hand.** The "mighty hand" brought Israel out (Deuteronomy 6:21) and later fought "against you … in anger" (Jeremiah 21:5).
> - **Fear.** One word, *yārēʾ*, "to fear", names the fear that drives a person away from God and the fear of God that keeps a person from sin. In one sentence Moses takes the first away and sets the second in its place: "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin" (Exodus 20:20). The same people, with the same word, are afraid of Egypt and then fear the Lord (Exodus 14:10, 31). Turned round, the word describes the one who is feared: "the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love" (Nehemiah 1:5). Beside a choice it has three more faces. It is learned at a feast in the place God chose: "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always" (Deuteronomy 14:23). It falls on those who hear of presumption punished: "all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13). And it comes as terror on people who resisted God's choice once he made it plain: "Are we all to perish?" (Numbers 17:13). Section 10.1 sets out the word, and 10.7 the faces beside a choice.
> - **"Do not fear."** God says it with a reason, and the reason is himself: "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10). Joseph says it and refuses to stand in God's place (Genesis 50:19, 21). Jael says it before the tent peg (Judges 4:18). The words are the same. What they are for is not.
> - **Trembling and dread.** The Hebrew words for trembling and dread are rendered as fear, and also as "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4), "deeply moved" (2 Samuel 18:33), a heart that "trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13), and "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5). I read them as naming one inner stirring, which its situation turns into fear, anger, grief, care or joy (10.1).
> - **"None shall make you afraid."** It is promised peace: "I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid" (Leviticus 26:6). The same Hebrew phrase is used of desolation: "The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid" (Isaiah 17:2). One phrase describes rest for a people and the emptiness left when they are gone.
> - **Care.** The Greek *merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care", is rebuked when it is about my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25) and praised when it is "genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20). The Hebrew *dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", is dread of what may come (Jeremiah 38:19), a father's worry for his son (1 Samuel 10:2), and sorrow for sin: "I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18). Section 10.1 sets this out.
> - **Hiding.** The Hebrew *sātar*, "to hide", is God hiding a person in safety and God hiding his face, four verses apart (Psalm 27:5, 9), and a sinner asking God to hide his face from his sins (Psalm 51:9). A treasure is hidden "in his joy", and a talent hidden because "I was afraid" (Matthew 13:44; 25:25). Sections 10.9 and 10.11.
> - **Murmuring.** The Hebrew *rāgan* is the people's complaint "in your tents" against God (Deuteronomy 1:27) and the whisperer's words that separate friends (Proverbs 16:28) (10.5).
> - **Remembering.** It bows the soul down and it gives hope, in two consecutive verses (Lamentations 3:20–21; Chapter 10.3).
> - **The bed.** It is the same place, but what happens there goes either way. "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
> - **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.** Joshua leaves the choice to the people's own sight: "if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day" (Joshua 24:15). The king honours an old man's sight: "whatever seems good to you" (2 Samuel 19:38). In Isaiah the measure is the Lord's: "you did what was evil in my eyes" (Isaiah 65:12). Section 10.7 sets this out.
> - **Knowing good and evil.** It is the child's knowing "how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isaiah 7:15). It is Barzillai's palate at eighty, with the same words: "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?" (2 Samuel 19:35). And it is the weighing of words in a dispute: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4).
> - **Refusing.** The Hebrew *māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise", is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing "the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" (8:6). Elihu uses it of refusing God's terms (Job 34:33). Job turns it on himself: "therefore I despise myself, and repent" (42:6).
> - **Choosing.** The Hebrew *bāḥar*, "to choose", is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), of a place to live (Deuteronomy 23:16), of a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), of wisdom over silver (Proverbs 16:16), and of a verdict (Job 34:4).
> - **Delight.** The Hebrew *ḥāpēṣ*, "to delight in", is the soul's own delight in what it chose: "their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). It is also the Lord's delight as the measure of a choice. That delight is not met when people "chose what I did not delight in" (65:12), and met in those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4). The noun *ḥēpheṣ* names his settled purpose: "he shall fulfill all my purpose" (Isaiah 44:28). It names what a man cares about, and that stops at his death: "what do they care for their houses after them" (Job 21:21).
> - **Good, said of the eye.** "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). "Bountiful" is literally "good" (10.6).
> - **God's delight in a person.** It is the thanks of the rescued: "he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (Psalm 18:19). It is the mockers' taunt over a sufferer: "let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8). The claim is the same. The sufferer does not answer the mockers; he answers God: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9) (13.1).
> - **An offering.** "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it" (Psalm 51:16). Three verses on: "then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings" (51:19). It is the same offering. Between the two stands "a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (51:17) (13.1).
> - **Being well pleased.** The Greek *eudokeō* is the Father's word over the Son: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). It is also Paul's word for weaknesses he had pleaded three times to lose: "I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities" (2 Corinthians 12:10). Between his pleading and his contentment stands the answer, "My grace is sufficient for you" (12:9) (10.1).
> - **Choosing a person.** God chooses "before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and "those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). People choose by what they can already see: "men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
> - **Holiness.** It is the purpose of being chosen: "that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). It is also a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts" (Colossians 3:12). The verses do not say how the two fit.
> - **Desire beside a choice.** The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose: "you may eat within your towns whenever you desire" (Deuteronomy 12:21). The same words for the soul's desire draw a Levite to that place: "he may come when he desires" (18:6). And the soul's delight goes with a wrong choice: "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
> - **Despising.** Michal "despised him in her heart" when she saw the chosen king dancing before the Lord (2 Samuel 6:16). The same verb describes the servant, "one deeply despised", before whom kings will bow (Isaiah 49:7). People despise the chosen people, judging that God has rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24). And the chosen people themselves "despised the pleasant land" (Psalm 106:24). Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.
> - **Knowing that a choice was made.** Peter's hearers know it, and a quarrel ends in silence: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you" (Acts 15:7, 12). Paul knows it of others from what he saw: "we know … that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power" (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen "though you do not know me" (Isaiah 45:4). The world hates the chosen "because they do not know him who sent me" (John 15:21).
> - **Precious.** The Hebrew *yāqār* is wisdom weighed above *"nothing you desire"* (Proverbs 3:15), the word *"rare in those days"* (1 Samuel 3:1), a visit kept *seldom* (Proverbs 25:17), *"the moon moving in splendor"* that entices a heart (Job 31:26–27), a name *"highly esteemed"* (1 Samuel 18:30), *"the lordly price"* set on a shepherd (Zechariah 11:13), and a son *"dear"* while spoken against (Jeremiah 31:20). The Greek *timios* is faith tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7), the blood of Christ (1:19), and the jewels of Babylon (Revelation 17:4). What differs is who values, what the thing is weighed against, and whether its worth is known: man does not know wisdom's worth (Job 28:13), and Saul would not give the esteem the others gave (1 Samuel 18:29–30). (10.6 *Precious*.)
> - **Imperishable.** The Greek *aphthartos* and its noun name what the dead are raised: "the dead will be raised imperishable" (1 Corinthians 15:52).
